en: This collection is the wondrous medicine of the Buddha and a scripture for saving the world. It can cause those who are ill to recover as soon as they take it;
even those who are blind, deaf, mute, or lame may attain healing through it. The Daoist Xiu of Siming has traveled extensively across the lakes and seas and has experienced this medicine fully;

there is nothing that has not proven efficacious. It is only fitting, therefore, that it be published to endure for future generations. Thus, I— [The text continues with the author's name and further details.]
Preface to the *Jewel Mirror of Humans and Devas* by Liu Fei of Lanting, on the full moon of the sixth month in the year Gengyin of the Shaoding era. Regarding the sequence of this work:
I have taken pleasure in composing it.
I have humbly heard that when the virtuous deeds of past masters fail to shine brightly upon the world, it is the fault of later students.

For instance, regarding even a single word or deed of the ancient worthies of the Three Teachings within the Buddha-dharma, although these may be recorded in stele inscriptions, biographies, official records, and various collected works, they remain scattered across the four quarters, making them impossible to fully know or survey. Consequently, their hidden virtues may well be on the verge of being lost.

I am ignorant. In the past, while traveling among the monastic communities, I have occasionally obtained [teachings] from the exhortations of venerable masters or sought them out through my own investigations.
Whatever could inspire one’s resolve or serve as a mirror for the world, I have recorded as I encountered it.

In total, there are several hundred sections, titled *The Precious Mirror of Humans and Devas*. I have not further categorized the individuals by rank nor arranged them in chronological order, following the example of Dahui.
Regarding such works as the *Zhengfayan zang* (Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma), in the past, practitioners of Chan never failed to take the teachings and the Vinaya as their primary task;

nor did those devoted to the teachings and the Vinaya ever fail to take Chan as their primary task. Even scholars of Confucianism and Daoism never failed to find mutual accord and realize the truth through them.
This was not like the present day, when each school specializes in its own gate and monopolizes its own excellence, only to disparage one another.
To disparage [the ancients] as being like water and fire that cannot coexist—alas! The conduct of the ancients was not difficult to practice;
it was simply that people were self-deprecating and believed the ancients were unattainable. Little do they realize that the ancients were just like people of today.
If one can rouse their own will within this context, how would they differ from the ancients? Now, I have carved their writings and expanded upon their teachings, wishing to demonstrate them.
May scholars of future generations know that there are the exemplary models of their predecessors; may they all reach the Way itself. May those of lofty intelligence not deride this.
Preface by the Śramaṇa Tánxiù of Sìmíng on the day of the formal commencement of the retreat in the third year of the Shàodìng era.
The Mirror of Humans and Devas:

Emperor Dezong of the Tang dynasty asked Dharma Master Tan Guang, "For what reason is a *saṃgha* called a 'jewel'? He replied, "A *saṃgha* possesses six types [of practitioners] who are designated as jewels.
First, those who attain sudden enlightenment regarding their own minds, transcending the mundane and entering the sacred, are named Chan-monks (*dhyāna-bhikṣu*). Second...

1. Those who practice the integration of understanding and conduct, remaining untainted by worldly currents, are called eminent monks (*gaoseng*). 2. Those who possess the three—precepts, concentration, and wisdom—and have great eloquence, are called preaching monks (*jiangseng*). 3.
Those whose views and learning are profound and authentic, citing the past to verify the present, are called literary monks (*wenzhang seng*). 4.

Those who understand causes and recognize effects, practicing both compassion and majestic authority together, are called administrative monks (*zhushi seng*). 5. Those who are diligent in their meritorious deeds and cultivate them extensively are called monks of spiritual cultivation (*jingshen seng*).

Because he was named "Holy Fetus" (Shengtai), he was granted the title of a permanent monk (*chang seng*). The Emperor was greatly pleased and subsequently issued an edict for the state-wide ordination of monks (*Tang Sengzhuan*).
Master Dashan was a high-ranking disciple of Mount Heng; he practiced the *Lotus Sūtra* meditation gate and attained the Samādhi of Compassion.
At that time, although Zheng Senggao, the Interior Historian of Hengyang, frequently praised the Master’s virtue whenever he encountered the County Magistrate Chen Zhengye, yet...
Zheng had almost no intention of showing him faith. One day, he and Chen went hunting together and surrounded a herd of deer.
Zheng said to Chen, "You once praised Master Dashan for possessing the power of the Samādhi of Compassion. How will this herd of deer fare today?
Chen immediately led several attendants and they chanted in unison: "Namo Dashan Chanshi. At that very moment, the herd of deer...
He ascended into the air and departed. Thereupon, the Interior Secretary (Naisi) bowed down in shame.

(From the Stone Inscription at Guoqing) Venerable Zuoxi, whose name was Xuanglang, was a native of Wushang. He studied under the master Tiangong Wei; having received the essential instructions from his teacher, he later took up residence among the crags and valleys.
Sometimes monkeys would come to hold his alms bowl; sometimes birds would arrive to listen to his preaching of the sutras. Only ten... [text ends]
He practiced the eight kinds of twelve dhūta ascetic virtues for thirty years. In these matters, he refined his conduct and cultivated his person entirely in accordance with the monastic regulations.
Thus Li Hua said: "In meditation, there is no private transmission and he did not perceive bodily forms; in precepts, they were pure and without blemish, requiring no external formalities.
He did not wait for a multitude to lecture, yet he taught others without weariness. His dwelling was a humble cottage, and his food lacked rich flavors. At night..."
He did not once vainly hold aloft a lamp without having searched through the sacred scriptures; he did not take a single step in vain without having gazed upon the holy countenance [of the Buddha].
For over forty years he wore a single *uttarāsaṅga*, and for the rest of his life he never changed his single *niṣīdana*.
He never preached a single word of the Dharma for the sake of profit, nor did he ever accept so much as a hair’s breadth of wealth for the sake of the Dharma. (From the Original Biography)
Chan Master Wuxiang of Mount Wutai paid homage to the Buddha and addressed the assembly, saying:
"When you see a clay image, you treat it as if you were pounding rice; you have no conscious thought of its significance.

You do not realize that within each of your own domains there is a Buddha of empty space—smaller than the smallest, yet more ancient than Śākyamuni and Guanyin—who day and night radiates light through the gates of your six sense faculties."
The light moves the earth. Within the four modes of deportment, they emerge together and enter together, never for a moment separated by even a hair’s breadth.
Why not learn the ritual to take this Buddha? Instead, you go about making a living upon a lump of clay. If you can take this Buddha as your object of veneration, [then you have found it].
This is precisely to pay homage to your own mind. Although your mind consists of inverted and deluded thoughts, from the very beginning until this very day, it has been vast and pure.
It was never deluded when lost, nor has it ever awakened when enlightened. It is no different from the Buddha-Tathāgata, lacking nothing whatsoever.
It is only because you are greedily attached to external conditions that there is arising and ceasing, and delusion and awakening.
If one can, in a single thought-moment, turn the light back upon itself, one is immediately identical to all the sages. Thus it is said: "The Buddha is within your own heart;
yet people seek him outwardly. Within they harbor a priceless treasure, yet they fail to recognize that their very life is at rest.

Furthermore, we do not see how Master Suixian of Huayan spoke of realizing the self-nature of the mind, such that in all present activities—whether moving or still—there is nothing that does not accord with it.
This accords with the principle of the fundamental nature; therefore, throughout the day I prostrate to the Buddha but do not form a conceptual assembly of prostrations.
Throughout the day I recite the Buddha’s name but do not form a conceptual assembly of mindfulness. Now tell me, what kind of assembly is this *Avataṃsaka*?
This is exactly like Sudhana entering the Vairocana Pavilion and realizing an inconceivable state of sovereign mastery. At the end, it says: "I..."
He traveled through one hundred and ten cities and attended upon fifty-three spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
He beheld various realms and heard various Dharma gates, yet none of them possessed any reality. It is like a person who, within a dream, sees all manner of things;

only after waking from sleep does he realize it was a dream. O virtuous practitioners of meditation (*dhyāna*), although Sudhana recognized this clarity within the dream, [he did not realize it was a dream while dreaming].

Brilliantly clear! Yet, as before, you have fallen back into the realm of darkness. If you possess the eye at the crown of your head and the talisman behind your elbow, then Śākyamuni and Maitreya are nothing but dried excrement;
Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are but ordinary worldlings; True Suchness and Nirvāṇa are but hitching posts for donkeys;
and the entire Great Canon of Teachings is but paper for wiping sores. What kind of pavilion is there that one could enter?
The realms can be realized. If one is perhaps unable to do so, then for now, go and pay a full prostration or even half a prostration within the dream of another.

(From the *Tongxing lu*) This was done at the place of National Teacher Shao of Tiantai. He was a native of Longquan. After receiving full ordination, he applied himself with determination to inquiry and study, yet he attained nothing extraordinary.

He entered [the monastery] and, upon arriving at Caoshan, merely joined the assembly. Thereupon, a monk asked Fayan, "How can one suddenly bring all conditions to rest throughout the twelve periods of the day?
Fayan said, "Does emptiness act as a condition for you? Or does form act as a condition for you?
If you say emptiness acts as a condition, then emptiness is fundamentally without conditions. If you say form acts as a condition, then form and mind are non-dual. Day by day...

"What fruit do you use as the condition for you? When Yaoshan heard this, he was struck with awe and attained realization. Later, another Chan practitioner asked, "What is one drop of water from Cao’s spring?
Fayan said, "It is one drop of water from Cao’s spring. Upon hearing this, Yaoshan attained great enlightenment.
Fayan said, "You shall greatly propagate my school; do not remain stagnant here. He then traveled to Tiantai, where he looked upon the mountain with the intention of making it his permanent home.
At that time, Wang Yanjun, the Prince Zhongyi of Wuyue, was serving as the Governor of Taizhou and had long heard of the Master's reputation.
The King once sent an envoy to welcome him and treat him with the etiquette due to a disciple. One night, the King dreamed that his neck was severed by someone;
filled with alarm and lingering doubt, he sought a decision from Daoshao. Daoshao said, "This is no ordinary dream. It signifies that the character for 'King' (王) shall soon have one dot removed.
The King said, "If this indeed comes to pass, I shall not forget the Buddha's grace. In the first year of the Gānyòu era of the Han dynasty, the King succeeded to the throne.

He was enfeoffed as Duke and honored as National Teacher. At that time, following the upheaval of the Huichang era, the teachings of the Tiantai Zhiyi had seen their eminent masters withdraw into obscurity, and most of his Dharma-treasures had flowed eastward across the sea.
Master Jikaku of Rakkei lamented that these teachings were on the verge of vanishing from hearing;
he exerted his strength to retrieve them. Previously, from the collection at Jinhua, he had managed to obtain only a single commentary on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*. Later, due to Zhong...

King Yi examined the Buddhist scriptures but was perplexed by their doctrinal characteristics, so he requested to consult with [Zhili] Shao. Shao praised Jizhong Ji for his profound mastery of the Tiantai Way.
Consequently, the King summoned Ji to establish a lecture series. The King was greatly pleased and specially dispatched ten envoys across the sea to transcribe and bring back the texts.
It is due to the efforts of these two masters, Shao and Ji, that the teachings were revived and have remained largely undiminished until the present day. (The fourth year of Kaibao)
On the twenty-eighth day of the sixth month of that year, he passed away peacefully on Mount Huading. That night, stars fell to the earth and a great snowstorm descended from the heavens.
The extraordinary signs accompanying the Master’s nirvana are too numerous to record in full; they are detailed in the *Record of the Conduct and Deeds of Chan Master Deng*.

The Master of Dhyāna, the Wise Zhiyi, addressed the assembly, saying: "Dharma Master Zhao, my fellow student at Mount Nanyue, was foremost among the multitude in his ascetic practices and meditative concentration.
He would habitually take a pinch of salt from the communal store for his own use as a drink during meals. Since the amount he took was so small, he did not consider it a matter of consequence.
Later, while performing the Fangdeng (Vaipulya) rites, he suddenly saw signs of retribution arise; by the end of three years, the increase had reached several tens [of pinches]."

One *hu* [of salt] was urgently required for compensation; furthermore, he had to sell his clothing and possessions to buy salt to repay the community. This matter did not take long to unfold, nor is it merely hearsay.
You should take this as a lesson and ensure that you do not regret it later. Although my own virtuous conduct is meager, people from far and near have come to seek me out quite frequently.
However, as the Shan Ling mountain range lies between us, it is difficult to travel on foot. For my old age and illness, I usually have a group of mules to escort me in and out.

If this were merely a private matter for my guests to calculate their own merit and reward, I would simply ensure that neither side incurs any fault. But since I am the master of the community, the mules are also mine to command.
"Once something has been relinquished and entered into the community, it is no longer mine; I ought not to use it. Since it is not mine, what more need be said?
This one principle applies to all other matters as well. (Guoqing Bailu).
Master Wulu of Tushita studied under Master Puning. He maintained himself with rigorous discipline, eating only one meal per day, and performed his prostrations...
He recited [the scriptures] without ceasing. Later, he resided at Tuṣita. He once asked Chan Master Lin of Mount Daojing about the path of the Dharma.

Upon seeing that he was so intent on observing the precepts that he did not penetrate the principles of the Way, Lin jokingly said to him, "Are you not stifled by the shackles of the Vinaya? Wugu replied:
Because his faculties and consciousness were dull and obscured, he could not help but remain bound. Hoping that the Master would take pity on him and instruct him, [Bodhidharma] spoke.

Bodhidharma then cited the case of Vāsukabandhu, who ate but one meal a day, never lay down to sleep, prostrated before the Buddha during the six periods of the day, and was pure and untainted, becoming a refuge for the masses.
When the twentieth patriarch, Jayata, wished to convert him, he asked his disciples: "This dhūta practitioner has cultivated the Brahma-faring with such diligence; can he be saved?"
The disciple said, "If one is as diligent as this, why should it not be possible? Yan-muo said, "Your master is far removed from the Way;
even if he were to pass through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, he would remain rooted in falsehood.

The disciple, unable to contain his indignation, said to Yan-muo, "What virtues does the Venerable One possess that you should disparage my master? Yan-muo replied, "I do not seek the Way, nor am I deluded."
I do not prostrate to the Buddha, yet I do not treat him with contempt. I do not sit in perpetual meditation, yet I am not indolent.
I do not eat only once a day, yet I do not eat at irregular intervals. I am neither contented nor greedy. That the mind has no object of attachment is called the Way.
Upon hearing this, Baoxiu attained untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*). Ling then let out a sharp, resonant shout and said, "Even if it were as you say, you would still be a dull-witted fellow.
At these words, Wugu’s mind was suddenly enlightened; leaping for joy, he prostrated and said, "Had I not heard the Master’s instruction, how could I have known my error?
From now on, I shall maintain that which is 'not maintained. By maintaining the unconditioned precepts (*anabhisaṃskāra-śīla*), there is no further need to apply the mind."
This was his power. When he took his leave and returned to the abbot’s quarters, he cast aside his former habits;

there remained only a single meditation seat, and apart from preaching the Dharma, he sat in silence. Suddenly, one night, he summoned the Dharma Master Mingjing and said, "I selected Wugu and obtained Jingshan, who shattered my emotional attachments.
To this day, not a single thing remains within me. Tonight, I wish to enter the soundless samādhi."
He departed. Thereupon, he remained in silence and eventually passed away into a long sleep (*Tongxing lu*).

During the True Doctrine Period (*Zhenzong*), the Emperor once intended to abolish Taiping Xingguo Temple to convert it into a granary. On the day the imperial edict was issued, a monk abruptly intervened, asserting that the temple must not be abolished.
The Emperor dispatched an imperial messenger with these instructions: "If you do not obey the order to abolish the temple, you shall be executed. Furthermore—

He brandished a sword at him and made a vow, saying: "If you, monk, show fear upon seeing the sword, I shall immediately execute you; otherwise, I shall spare you. The imperial messenger followed these instructions.
The monk laughed and extended his neck, saying: "To die for the sake of the Buddha-dharma is truly a sweet thing to savor.

The Emperor was pleased, and the monastery was consequently spared from destruction. Han Zicang said: "In the present age, only a monk such as this may truly be called a 'patch-robed disciple' (nàzǐ). (*Shímén jí*)

Chan Master Fachang Yu was a native of Gaoting in Linzhang. Having left home as a youth, he possessed great aspirations; he traveled through various regions until his fame resounded throughout the monastic centers.
Master Fushan Yuan pointed him out to others, saying, "This is a model for future students who travel on pilgrimage.
Later, in the north of Fenning, amidst a thousand peaks and ten thousand ravines among old houses and ruined walls, Yu settled there. From time to time, disciples would arrive to visit him.
They all found their labors bitter; he never once used a single word of indirectness to instruct his disciples.
The students could not understand his intent, nor could they share in his serene detachment and hardships, so they all departed.

For this reason, he remained a solitary dweller on the mountain, never ceasing until old age to offer morning incense, evening lamps, ascend the hall, and preach the Dharma. This is how it was in the monastic groves.
His robes and articles of use were all complete. Xu Xi of Longtu sighed and said, "To have no assembly yet to have an assembly—this is truly a man who dwells in the mountains in his true colors.
On the day before his passing, he encountered [Xu] and left him a verse, saying: "This year I am seventy-seven; When going out, one must choose an auspicious day.
Last night I informed Guige, Announcing that tomorrow morning will be lucky. Xu read the verse and was struck with awe; he invited Lingyuan [to his residence].
They went together. Upon arriving there, [the master] was already in a state of profound stillness.

(From the *Tingjiang ji*) Venerable Fazhi, whose name was Zhili, remained in the constant sitting posture (*prahāṇa*) without lying down from the age of forty. His feet never ventured outside, and he sent away all visitors who came to pay their respects.
One day, he said to his disciples: "For half a verse, one may forget one's body; for a single phrase, one may cast oneself into fire. This is the way of the Sage..."
"The mind regarding the Dharma is thus. I cannot abandon my body and life to rouse those who are indolent; how could such a thing even be worth mentioning?
Thereupon, he gathered ten monks to practice the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*, vowing that at the completion of three years, they would all immolate their bodies together.

At that time, Yang Yi of the Hanlin Academy sent a letter earnestly requesting him to remain in the world, further raising difficult questions based on the sentiments of worldly delight and renunciation. Venerable...

The respondent replied: "Throughout the day one deconstructs marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and yet all dharmas are established; throughout the day one establishes dharmas and yet not even a speck of dust remains.
Master Yang again posed a question: "The wind whistles through the jeweled trees and the waves ripple the golden lotuses—what kind of person’s realm is this?"

The respondent replied, "There is simply no further principle to this matter of seeing and hearing. The Duke asked again, "In both the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*, it is said that these were spoken by Māra.
The respondent answered, "How far apart are Buddha and Māra? The Duke realized that he could neither be subdued by logic nor detained by words;
he therefore sent a letter to Ciyun (Zhiyuan), requesting him to come from Hangzhou to Mingzhou in person to dissuade him from his views. Furthermore...

He entrusted the local governor with its protection so that it could not be burned. In that year, the Master requested a posthumous title from the court. Emperor Zhenzong summoned Yang to inquire about him; the Master then reported on the matter of the Master’s physical remains. The Emperor praised and sighed in admiration, and addressed Yang again with great earnestness, saying: [The Emperor said: "I have heard that the Master was a man of extraordinary virtue and a vessel of the Way. His teachings have spread far and wide, and his influence has reached even the present day. It is fitting that he be honored with a posthumous title. He then conferred upon him the title "Great Master of the True Source" (Zhenshoulu Daoshi). Furthermore, the Emperor issued an imperial decree stating: "The Master’s remains shall be enshrined within the temple grounds, and a memorial tablet shall be erected to commemorate his legacy. Thus, the Master’s spirit was revered by both the sovereign and the people. His influence extended through successive generations, and his reputation remained unblemished throughout the ages. This is truly a rare occurrence in the history of our nation. May this account serve as a testament to the profound efficacy of the Buddhist Dharma. "Simply convey my intent: I request to remain in this world. I shall grant you the title 'Dharma-Wisdom' (Fazhi). Consequently, his vows and practices could no longer be fulfilled.
He then cultivated the *Guangming* Repentance as a preparatory rite for his passing. On the fifth day, while sitting in the lotus posture, he summoned the assembly and said:
"When a person is born, they must inevitably die; this is simply the constant law of nature. You all should diligently cultivate the Way without allowing for any interruption.
Following my instructions is equivalent to following me in life. Having finished speaking, he recited the Buddha’s name and passed away. (From the *Jiaoxinglu* and other sources.

Chan Master Wontong Ne was a native of Zizhou. His character was upright and serene. He maintained order among his followers with proper method and disciplined himself with rigorous austerity. At night...

He would invariably enter meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Initially, his hands were folded naturally; by midnight, they gradually rose until they reached his chest. His attendant would observe this every time to gauge the arrival of dawn.
Emperor Renzong heard of his fame and issued an imperial decree for him to reside at Jingyin Monastery. Zhenne declined on the grounds of illness and recommended Zhili to serve as his successor.

When summoned for an audience, the Emperor was greatly pleased and bestowed upon him the title of Chan Master Dajue. During the reign of Emperor Yingzong, he was once granted a personal imperial edict. Tian...
The lower temple was occupied by its incumbent abbot according to his own will, and Liaan said nothing about it; few people were aware of this.
When Dongpo composed the inscription for the Chenkui Pavilion, he sent a letter to inquire about it, stating: "I have already completed the draft for the inscription of the Chenkui Pavilion.

Being frail and having long abandoned my studies, I do not know if it is worthy of being carved upon stone. I heard from Chan Master Canliao that on the day you left the capital, Emperor Ying bestowed a handwritten imperial edict upon you."

The summary states: "As for 'abiding in the natural disposition' (*zhenxing zhuchi*), I do not know whether it is correct or not. I earnestly request that you provide the full text so that I may include this section.
Lia replied that he did not have it, but later Jie found it among his books. Su Dongpo remarked upon hearing this:

"Were it not for a man who has attained the Way, how could such refinement (*yunjie*) exist? The Record of the Su Pavilion states: "Although the Master had left the mundane world to deliver sentient beings..."

He maintained the Vinaya with extreme rigor. When the Emperor presented him with a camphor bowl, the Master burned it before the messenger, saying, "In our Dharma, one wears dyed robes and eats from earthenware bowls;
this bowl is contrary to the Dharma. When the messenger returned and reported this, the Emperor marveled at his virtue.
After a long time, the Master’s dwelling and his personal effects were such that they could have been used to transform the site into a magnificent monastery; yet he did nothing of the sort.
He established a vihāra only to the west of the capital, capable of accommodating barely a hundred people.
Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty asked Master Zhigong, "In my leisure time from the myriad affairs of state, I cultivate various virtuous deeds.

Do these possess merit and virtue or not? Zhigong replied, "They do have merit, but they are not true merit. The Emperor asked, "What is meant by 'true'? Zhigong said, "The nature is pure and the mind is luminous;
its essence is inherently empty and still—this is true merit. Thereupon, the Emperor attained realization. Thus, as the former sages have said:
If one can sit in meditation for even a single moment, it surpasses the construction of stupas made of the seven treasures as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Those stupas will ultimately turn to dust; yet, through a single thought of pure mind, one attains perfect enlightenment.

(From the *Tongxing lu*) The Realized Man Sun Simiao was a native of Jingzhao. From childhood he was intelligent and wise, reciting ten thousand words daily. He was skilled in the *Zhuangzi* and *Laozi*, and was particularly devoted to them.

Zhì devoted himself to the exegesis of the Buddhist scriptures. He lived to the age of one hundred and fifty years. He once lived in seclusion on Mount Zhongnan, abstaining from food and drink and consuming only lead and mercury.
He was a close friend of Vinaya Master Xuán, with whom he would engage in discussion all day long. He once transcribed the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

At that time, Emperor Taizōng of the Táng dynasty wished to read Buddhist scriptures and asked Huìmāo which sūtra was the greatest; Māo replied, "The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is the most honored and supreme among the Buddha’s teachings."
The Emperor said, "Recently, Tripitaka Master Xuanzang translated the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* in six hundred fascicles;
why is that not considered great, while this [text] of eighty fascicles is still regarded as great? He replied, "The Dharma-realm of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* encompasses all gates;
within a single gate, one may manifest sūtra scrolls as vast as a great trichiliocosm. The *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* is but a single gate of the *Avataṃsaka*. " The Emperor was enlightened.
From this point on, receive and uphold [this teaching]. (From the *Shishi lue shuo*).

A letter sent by Palace Attendant Yang Yi to the Secretariat Drafter Li Wei, in which it says in brief: "While serving as the temporary governor of Nanchang, I happened to meet the Chan Master Guanghui.
With my official duties simplified and ample leisure after the midday meal, he would sometimes come at my invitation while I sat in meditation, or I would mount my carriage to follow him."
I requested to question him on matters without fixed direction, and my obscurations and stagnations were instantly resolved. After half a year, I was vast and free from doubt;

it was as if having forgotten something and suddenly remembering it, or as if having slept and suddenly waking. The things that had long obstructed my chest fell away with a sudden crash, and matters unclarified for kalpas appeared vividly before me.
Thus, my discernment became thoroughly penetrating and my engagement with the world free from impediment. Reflecting deeply upon this, I pondered:
The former masters mostly engaged in extensive seeking and inquiry. For example, Xuefeng went up to Dongshan nine times and to Touzi three times, eventually succeeding Deshan.
Linji received the Dharma from Dayu, yet ultimately inherited Huangbo. Yunyan frequently received instruction and guidance from Daowu, and thus became a disciple of Yaoshan.
Danxia personally received the seal of approval from Mazu, yet became a follower of Shitou.

They are his descendants; in antiquity there were many such, and in principle there is no cause for objection. My illness lies in the fact that my current karmic conditions for succession truly depend upon Guanghui, while the source of my inspiration and exhortation truly comes from Aofeng.
I am filled with joy at the opportunity to discuss the Way with you, monks.
The Vice Minister then remarked, "In general, those who study the Way must always maintain vigilance throughout the twelve periods of the day; one must not merely talk about Chan and the Way."
At that moment, there is a principle of maintaining constant awareness. This must not be absent even during daily activities.
It is like a hen brooding her eggs; if she abandons them and leaves, the warmth will not be sustained and they will fail to hatch.
Now, amidst the myriad phenomena surrounding us and the restless agitation of the six sense organs, to lose even a moment of care is to risk losing one's very life. This is no small matter.
Now you have come to undergo this dependent origination and are bound by birth and death.

This is because for kalpas as numerous as dust motes, you have followed the mind of arising and ceasing, flowing along with others until the present day. Everyone, tell me: if you had once lost it, how could you have reached this point?
Do you wish to recognize the white ox on the open ground right now? Try pulling its nose-strap and see! It is also said, "Śākyamuni..."
On the occasion of the assembly at Vulture Peak, Kāśyapa looked toward Mahākāśyapa and said to the great multitude, "I have the Eye of the True Dharma and entrust it to Mahākāśyapa.
He further said, "Throughout forty-nine years, I have not uttered a single word. What is the principle behind this?
If it were within the sphere of ordinary people, they would be unable to place even a single footstep upon it. This is because...
Each of you possesses something extraordinary; yet to call it "extraordinary" is already incorrect.
I say that Śākyamuni was a defeated general, and Kāśyapa was one who lost his body and his life.
How do you understand this? Have you not heard it said: "Nirvana and birth-and-death are both but dream-words; Buddhas and sentient beings are equally [empty] designations."
I say: You must understand it directly like this; do not run outward in pursuit. If you have not yet clarified this point, I dare say that everyone’s deviation from the truth is no small matter.
One day before his passing, the Minister personally wrote a verse for his family, instructing them to deliver it to Prince Li the following day.
The verse says: "The arising of bubbles and the ceasing of bubbles—these two dharmas are fundamentally..."
Come to Qi. If you wish to know the place of true refuge, it is east of Zhaozhou’s East Monastery and west of its West Monastery. The Prince Consort received this verse, which says:
"Selling paper money in the Temple of Mount Tai. (From the *Tiansheng Guangdeng Lu*).
Duke Zhang Wending was a monk who served as the Librarian at Langye in a previous life; he died before he had finished copying the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, after which he made a vow.
He said, "I shall write again when I am born in the next life. Later, while serving as the Prefect of Chuzhou, he went to travel at Mount Langya.

As he paced back and forth along the corridors, he found it particularly difficult to leave. Suddenly, in the lower section of the monastery, he experienced a sudden awakening. Pointing to a scripture case between the beams, he said, "This is the matter of my previous life."
He had it brought and examined; it was indeed the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*. Its calligraphy was no different from that of the copy he had made during his lifetime.

Once, as he read the passage: "The world is free from arising and ceasing, like flowers in the sky; wisdom perceives neither existence nor non-existence," he gave rise to a heart of great compassion and subsequently clarified his own realization with this verse:
"A single thought-moment harbors arising and ceasing; A thousand mechanisms bind one to existence and non-existence. The divine blade is light..."

Regarding the origin: [Zhaozhou] passed through and emerged from the revolving bowl-bead. In his later years, he produced this sutra and showed it to the layman Dongpo (Su Shi), while also recounting the circumstances of its composition to him.
Su Shi inscribed a postscript on it, which was carved into stone at Mount Jinshan.
Chan Master Qin was a native of Longcheng in the state of Qin. Initially, he received the Dharma from Master Tiansheng Tai; later, he relied upon Chan Master Huanglong Nan.
Seeing that what Qin had attained was precise and correct, Nan treated him with great favor and ordered him to reside at Xingguo Temple in Quan to open the hall for formal preaching.
He subsequently became the dharma-heir of Nan. One night, he dreamed that a deity told him: "Master, when you encounter a malignant disease, it shall be your karmic condition."

When he had finished speaking, he vanished. Thirteen years later, Bai Guo fell ill with leprosy (*mahāvātavyādhi*). He withdrew from monastic affairs and returned to the west of Longcheng to build a small hermitage.

Once the hermitage was completed, he stayed there to nurse his illness. He had a junior disciple named Ke Ci, who had long relied upon Yangqi and was also an outstanding figure within the Chan forest.
Ke Ci returned to attend to his master’s illness; he served him with the utmost filial piety, begging for food in the villages while the wind... [blows].
He endured rain, cold, and heat, exhausting his efforts throughout his life before finally passing away. One day, Zhiqin said to Cui: "That which I have attained truly comes from Master Tian-sheng.
Later, seeing that Huanglong’s Way and conduct were both profound and weighty, I felt deep reverence and admiration, and thus became his successor.

Who would have thought that for half my life I was afflicted by this foul disease? Now, fortunately, it has reached its full term. In the past, many immortals and transcendents [attained their goals] because of such misfortunes..."
He attained the Way of the Immortals with such swiftness because he severed his worldly entanglements and cherished the spirit of the Yingyang tradition;
thus, it was through misfortune that he brought about good fortune. Had I not gained this victory through this dispute, I would not have the situation I have today.
Now, whether I hold fast or let go is up to me; whether I restrain or release, I possess total mastery. Thereupon, he sighed once. After a long while...
He passed away. Upon his cremation, a rare fragrance pervaded the wilds, and countless śarīras were produced.

(From the *Zhufeng Lu*) The head seat Xiyán, whose courtesy name was Shèngtú, possessed a nature that was firm and decisive. He was well-versed in both Buddhist and secular learning and maintained himself with integrity and high principles.

Having completed his travels, he returned to live in seclusion at his old dwelling. His footsteps never entered the mundane world; he frequently remained in meditative seclusion behind closed doors. This was because his conduct and character were exceptionally pure and noble.
No one should be his companion. Renowned officials and noblemen repeatedly invited him with offers of various monasteries, yet he steadfastly did not respond.

At that time, there was a novice named Canji who wished to serve as an attendant to the Master. Yan recognized that he was not a fit vessel and composed a "Treatise on Resolving Difficulties" to decline him, saying:
"One knows one's son as no other can; one knows one's father as no other can. As for my Canji, he is not..."

To become a vessel for the Sangha—how could such renunciation and entry into the monastic order be a trivial matter? It is not for the sake of seeking ease and comfort; it is not for the sake of seeking warmth and fullness;
it is not for the sake of seeking the profit and fame that are as small as the tip of a snail's horn. It is for the sake of birth and death; it is for the sake of sentient beings;

it is for the sake of severing afflictions, crossing the ocean of the triple world, and continuing the Buddha’s life of wisdom. The time since the Sage departed is remote and the Buddha-Dharma is greatly in decline. How dare you...
To act thus is delusory. The *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* states: "If a bhikṣu does not cultivate the dharma of a bhikṣu, there is not even enough space for a single drop of spittle in the great trichiliocosm.
The *Tonghui Lu* says: "If one serves the Sangha without being included among the ten categories [of monastic duties], serving the Buddha is merely a labor in vain.

Would it not be difficult to achieve this even after a hundred years? Judging by this, I have already improperly joined the ranks of the clergy and brought reproach upon the Buddha; how much more so is this the case for you? Nevertheless...
Having left the household life to become a monk, if one does not understand the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings, does not clarify the Way of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius,
does not comprehend cause and effect, does not penetrate one’s own nature, does not know the hardships of plowing and harvesting,

and does not reflect upon how it is difficult to digest offerings of faith, then one merely drinks wine and eats meat, breaking the fast and violating the precepts; engaging in trade and commerce, practicing theft and deceit, gambling at games, and coveting monastic dwellings.
They travel with canopies borne before them and receive offerings for their own sake alone—how tragic! To possess a body six feet tall yet lack wisdom, the Buddha calls such a person a "deluded monk.
To have a tongue three inches long yet be unable to preach the Dharma, the Buddha calls such a person a "dumb sheep."
Appearing to be monks yet not being monks, appearing to be laypeople yet not being laypeople—Buddha called them "monks like birds and mice," and they are also termed "shaven-headed householders.
Therefore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* asks: "What are these thieves who, donning my robes, deceive and trade upon the Tathāgata? They create all manner of karmic deeds;
they are not the ships that ferry across the world, but rather seeds for the hells. Even if Maitreya were to descend to be born and one were to obtain a human head, [it would still be so]."
Their bodies have already fallen into the hundredfold agonies of the Iron Ring Mountains; this has not been for a single morning or evening.
If those who act now were to do so by the hundreds, thousands, or even tens of thousands, they would merely be a mass of physical forms and attire. What substance could there be within them?
This is what is meant by "having the feathers of a hawk yet the cry of a phoenix. Common stones are not jade; the spreading of *xiāo* grass and the flourishing of *ài* weeds are not snow.
Mountains are the place for the herb of patience. The state’s ordination of monks was originally intended to pray for blessings.

Now, conversely, they are made to pay taxes in the form of *dingqian* (poll tax), demonstrating to the people that the clergy are not like them. This brings our followers to such a state of insufficiency.
It is just as the case of the single fox-wing among the feathers of the former-day Yuyang Liaoyuan, Yong’an Songlongjing Jingling Zhiyao; as for the rest, it is merely the skin of a thousand sheep.
What need is there to speak further? Alas! The filth and dregs within the ocean of the Buddha’s teachings have never been as severe as they are today.
This can be discussed with the wise; it is difficult to speak of it with worldly people.

Dharmatrāta was a native of Jiahe. Having renounced his home, he went to pay his respects to Dharma Master Shenwu. Dharmatrāta was fully endowed with both scriptural learning and spiritual practice, serving as a donor of the Dharma.
In his later years, he resided at Beichen Monastery. Once, while begging for food in the marketplace, someone told him to stop;

Dharmatrāta said, "The legacy of the former Buddhas must be practiced in this degenerate age; it is no trivial matter. In governing himself and leading the assembly, Dharmatrāta maintained complete discipline and propriety. Therefore, his...
The formal protocols of his Dharma assemblies were preeminent in the region west of the Zhejiang River. He once instructed his disciples, saying:

"Within the twelve periods of the day and throughout the four modes of deportment, there are always dharmas to be employed. If you do not investigate with a focused mind and act according to what is taught, every movement will become a demonic activity.
Furthermore, when the alms bowl is set out, the spirits and ghosts of the wilderness often suffer from hunger; they hear the bhikṣu strike the bowl."

The sound further increases the fire of hunger, making the suffering even more severe. Therefore, the Buddha issued a warning: one must first bring body and mind to stillness before receiving food offerings.
Thus, the Pure Rules (Qinggui) include a prayer for the water discarded from the bowl, which says: *Oṃ ma-hū-ra-śe svāhā*.

Even those who single-mindedly transmit the Mind-Seal (the Chan masters of Baizhang’s lineage) still observe such minute practices; how much more so should we, the ancestors, who are proficient in both the Mind-Seal and the Vinaya?

This is the teaching [of the Buddha]. You must be especially careful not to neglect this when bathing. In the past, there was a bhikṣu who, while bathing, laughed and played instead of maintaining right mindfulness;
he later received the retribution of being splashed with boiling water. Therefore, the former sages instructed one to bind the mind and observe.
Always make a vow as you speak: "As I now bathe my body, I vow that all sentient beings shall be free from defilement in body and mind, radiant and pure both internally and externally.
These two lines apply to all other matters as well. Do you not feel a sense of urgency and diligence in your daily lives?
"Retreating to reflect upon my own conduct, I have made good use of my mind.

(From the *Tongxing lu*). Master Ciyun Shi said: "I was a friend to Fazi of Siming for over forty years, yet at the time of his passing, I was unable to weep even once beneath the door of his chamber. Unable to exhaust my lamentations, I composed this verse, which says:"
In the heavens there is no moon that is its peer; among men there is but this one monk. Let those who read this not say that I am partial toward what I know and dismissive of what I do not know;
I have merely observed that his understanding and practice possess a distinction that stands far above others, and thus I have used these extreme words to express my sentiments.
What is it that makes him so extraordinary? Within the various divisions of the teachings of our school, he has recorded everything that the Master of Pilin had not previously recorded.
He practiced the four samādhis, all of which are difficult for others to perform. Although cold and heat alternated, he did not let his side touch the mat for sixty-nine years until his death.
Despite being so ill and infirm, there was no interruption in his practice of the Way or his preaching and instruction.
When his disciples invited him to a banquet, he did not comply. Upon his death, the number of his *śarīra* relics was unknown. Alas! It is not difficult to know; it is the practice that is difficult.
Chan Master Longhu Wen was the crown prince of Emperor Xizong of the Tang dynasty. His features and bone structure were as pure and elegant as a painting. Emperor Xizong—
He cherished him deeply; yet, because [the latter] lacked any intention to engage with the world, despite a hundred attempts at molding and guiding him, he ultimately could not be turned back.

He only admired the style of Shuanghua (Huijiao), yearning to see him in his dreams. In the first year of the Zhonghe era, when the empire was in great chaos, he finally cut off his hair and wandered away as a recluse.
No one recognized him. When he visited Shishuang Chanshi, the Master spoke with him and sighed, saying, "You were born into a royal family by the power of your vows;

to have left it all behind to follow me is truly like a lotus blooming in the midst of fire. At night, he heard [the Master] enter his room and earnestly asked, "Are you willing to entrust me with the matter of the Patriarchs' separate transmission?
Shishuang said, "Do not slander the Patriarchs. [Zhaozhou] replied, "The world's foremost patriarch..."
"How magnificent this intent is! Could it have been devised by mere whim? He said, "Wait until you see Mount Shan nod its head, and I shall tell you.

Having heard this, he took his leave that very day. Upon reaching the outskirts of Shaowu City, he saw the mountain rising with deep and elegant beauty; he then pushed aside the grass and pressed forward.
He saw an ascetic hidden within it and, with joyful deference, offered him his hut, saying, "Venerable sir, you should flourish here.
He then performed a long bow and departed, his destination unknown. Having heard this, [Huiyuan] settled there for over ten years. One day, an old man came to visit him and said:
"I am no human; I am a dragon. Because I failed in my duty regarding the rain, Heaven has meted out punishment. I rely on the power of the Way to escape it.

Thereupon, he transformed into a small snake and crawled into his sleeve. At night, wind and thunder seized the sitting platform, and the mountains shook with such violence that one would have expected danger, yet [the Master] sat upright as if nothing were happening.
When dawn broke and the weather cleared, the snake fell to the ground and departed. Shortly thereafter, an old man came to offer his thanks.
He said, "It was not by the power of a Great Being that this mountain was made foul with blood and stench.

Thinking there was no way to repay such profound virtue, I shall hollow out beneath this cliff to create a spring. In the future, when many people lack water, this will be the reason for inviting you, Master.
The spring has now become a lake, and it is named after him. (From the Temple Record Stele)
Chan Master Zhixi once traveled with Master Fushan Yuan. He frequently established a hermitage at Foshouyan on Mount Lu.

Later, he went to Mount Siming, where he lived in solitude for over ten years. Even when tigers and leopards appeared before him, he showed no sign of fear due to his power of meditative concentration.
He once said: "On the narrow paths frequented by birds, no one else arrives; amidst the silent clouds, there is but this single person. Thereafter...

Both monastics and laypeople heard of his reputation and admired him. He resided on the mountain for over forty years, living with such detachment that he possessed not even a hair’s breadth of personal accumulation.
Wearing only a single cotton robe throughout both winter and summer, he made the founding of the monastery his sole mission.

Through diligent effort and accumulation, he brought the Zen forest to completion, providing everything necessary for the community. Yet, he alone did not build a private chamber, choosing instead to dwell together with the assembly; for the Master...

He had intended to establish it as a place of private retreat and ease. However, the administrator Zhiyun, observing his own situation and waiting for the Master to travel far away, secretly built it for him.
When Chan Master Daguan Ying, who was then presiding over Xuedou, heard of this, he sighed and said: "Were it not for a true master of the school, there could be no such excellent assistant;
were it not for such an excellent assistant, the Way could not be honored. This is due to the virtue of the Master. (From the Inscription for Dazhang Xi)
The Dharma Master Biancai Jing was a native of Yushan in Hangzhou. At birth, a fleshy protuberance arose on his left shoulder like the cord of a *kāṣāya* robe;
it disappeared after eighty-one days. His father sighed and said, "This child is a śramaṇa from a previous life. Do not thwart his vow; he shall serve the Buddha in his adulthood.
When the Master’s teacher passed away, it was exactly at eighty-one years of age—this was likely his destined lifespan. After he had left the household life, whenever he saw...

Sitting upon the Dharma-seat, he sighed and said, "My wish is to ascend this seat to preach the Dharma and deliver sentient beings. He first visited Ciyun, where he applied himself with diligence day and night to the advancement of both study and practice.
Within a few years, he had reached the level of his senior disciples. After Ciyun passed away, he served Mingzhi Shao.

When Shao was lecturing on the *Mohe Zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation) at the section on the five conditions for the "expedient means," he cited the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*: "As Vimalakīrti said, 'With a single meal, one gives to all. He offered...
"One may eat only after first making offerings to the Buddhas and the assembly of worthy sages.

Upon hearing this, the Master attained enlightenment and said, "Today I have come to know that form, sound, fragrance, and flavor are inherently endowed with the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*). From this point on, I shall encounter all things without doubt.

At that time, Lord Shen Shucucai was governing Hangzhou; he considered the practice of reciting sutras and performing repentance rituals at the Guanyin Monastery to be the Buddha's work, rather than the practice of *dhyāna*.

He settled there and commissioned a master to teach him the transition from meditation to the *Yì* (Change). When the master arrived in Wúyuè, people flocked to him as if a Buddha had appeared in the world;
they served him as they would care for their own parents. Offerings of gold and silk came to him unsought. He resided at Tiānzhú for fourteen years.
Those who profited from his wealth pressured him to leave. The Master joyfully departed and did not harbor any resentment.
The assembly of Indian followers dispersed in all directions. When this matter was reported to the court, the following year an edict was issued for him to return to his former position.

The Master returned with reluctance, as if he had no choice. The assembly gathered once more in great numbers. Lord Zhao Qingxian was a friend of the Master beyond the mundane world; upon seeing [him], he...
He praised him, saying: "When the Master departed from India, the mountains were empty and the ghosts wept. Now that the Master has returned to India, the site of the Way shines with radiance.

He remained there for another two years. One day, he addressed the assembly, saying: "Our ancestor, the Sage Zhiyi, was a holy man; yet because he was so urgent in converting others, it hindered his own practice.
His rank was originally that of an Iron-Wheel King, yet his realization only reached the level of the Five Grades. How much more so for an ordinary person like myself?"
Thus he departed. He grew old upon the Dragon Well of the Southern Mountains, covering himself with thatch and bamboo. He closed his door and sat in meditation, remaining silent all day long.
His leaves fell while his roots flourished, like a withered tree in winter; his wind was upright and his waves stilled, like the waters of an ancient ravine.
Therefore, people named him "The Stammerer. His teacher was strict regarding the observance of the Vinaya. He lectured regardless of day or night, once saying:
"The spirits and deities lack sufficient majestic power and thus fear humans; if one lectures during the day, they may not be able to attend. Only when the night is still can they perhaps listen.
He once burned three fingers on his left hand and two on his right as an offering to the Buddha, barely managing to hold them. When a disciple wished to emulate him, [the Master stopped him].
[He] would always forbid [others], saying, "Only if it is like mine may it be acceptable. One day Dongpo said to him, "How many practitioners are there at Beishan who follow your way?

The Master replied, "The number of monks and secret practitioners is great; it is beyond what Yuanjing can fathom. (From the *Miscellaneous Steles of Longjing*) Chan Master Furong Kai addressed the assembly, saying:
"This mountain monk’s conduct and practice are not worthy of praise, yet I have the misfortune of presiding over this mountain gate. Now, wishing to..."

Briefly following the precedents established by past masters for the conduct of an abbot, and in order to collectively repay the Buddha’s kindness, we have deliberated with all concerned and resolved that I shall no longer descend the mountain, attend formal meals, or dispatch emissaries for fundraising.
Instead, I shall take the annual revenue from the monastery’s estates and divide it into three hundred and sixty equal portions.
One portion shall be drawn daily for use, without increasing or decreasing the amount at the request of others. This may be done.
If rice is available, prepare rice; if rice is insufficient, prepare gruel; if gruel is insufficient, prepare rice-soup.
For newly arrived guests, there shall be only tea and soup upon meeting. One must strive to minimize external conditions and focus exclusively on practicing the Way. Even so, this is the case.
Furthermore, it is up to each of you to judge according to seniority. This mountain monk cannot force it upon you either.
Gentlemen, have you seen the verse of the ancients? "Mountain rice with unhusked millet; wild greens with plain yellow pickles. If you will eat them, eat as you please."
"Do not eat, yet let things come as they may.
(Recorded Sayings) Master Zhizhe of Zhi Mountain addressed the assembly, citing an ancient worthy who, while residing on a mountain, always ordered the cook to prepare congee.
One day, as the cook watched the fire consuming the wood, he realized that every thought-moment brings exhaustion; the transition of impermanence is thus all the more swift. Thereupon—
Before the hearth, he entered silent meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and did not emerge for several days. Upon rising, he went to the Elder (*sthavira*) and fully recounted what he had realized;
he described how the Dharma had become increasingly profound. The Elder said, "Everything you previously spoke of was within my own domain, but what you have now described is beyond my knowledge.
Do not speak of it further. He then asked, "Have you attained the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*)? He replied, "I know a little. He asked again, "In what way?"
[Question: "How can one who has committed such base offenses as sin attain awakening through merit? [Answer: "In a past life, he once resided on this mountain.

Because a guest arrived and encroached upon the small amount of vegetables belonging to the community, he was censured for this and has now become a slave to the assembly. Since his former habits have not yet been forgotten, he attains awakening easily.
(Guoqing Bailu)
The Bhikṣu of Great Wisdom and Righteous Dharma is properly named [Name]. In Sanskrit he is called *bhikṣu*; in the language of China, he is called "the Beggar" (*qǐshì*).
Internally, he begs for the Dharma to moisten his nature; externally, he begs for food to sustain his body. His parents, the most intimate of kin, were the first to be relinquished;
his beard and hair, which people hold dear, were entirely shaved away. Wealth overflowing with the seven treasures was discarded as if it were mere grass.

The mustard seed is of the most noble and honored rank; yet one regards it as no more than smoke or clouds. Reaching the ultimate weariness with impermanence, one deeply investigates the root of existence.
To elevate one’s aspirations, one must humble one’s person: holding the mendicant’s staff resembles a withered *li* plant; carrying the alms bowl is no different from a broken vessel;
