He left the mountain and sat in meditative repose for the entire day. This continued for nine years. One day he thought to himself, "I have lived here for a long time, yet no one has ever come.

My original intention was to benefit sentient beings; what is the use of living alone? He wished to abandon his hermitage and depart. Upon reaching the mouth of the valley, tigers, leopards, snakes, and pythons were blocking the path.
The Master said, "If I am destined to have a karmic connection with this place, may you all disperse. Otherwise, follow me."
"Eat this. Having spoken, they dispersed. Thereupon, [the master] returned. A deity saw him and said, "This mountain was once an araṇya during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha;
it shall now be restored as such. I shall constantly protect this mountain, for I have received a prophecy from the Buddha.
The following year, Dà'ān led a multitude and assisted in establishing the religious community (the temple stele).
Chan Master Jingyin Zhen was born in Gutian, Fuzhou. He received the essential instructions from Fushan Yuancong and later visited Jingyin Liaoyuan.
Master Liaoyuan appointed him as the head of the assembly; when Liaoyuan returned to Wu, Zhen succeeded him on the seat.

Emperor Shenzong once summoned him to the Qingshou Palace, where a high seat was prepared for him to engage in question-and-answer sessions with the public. Those present, both high and low, found such an experience unprecedented.

Zhen was a man of pure and profound character; he was dignified, serene, and retiring, appearing as though he could not speak. Yet when it came to debate and exposition, his eloquence was sweeping and unhindered.
He lived with extreme simplicity; for twenty years he wore a single cotton skirt without changing it. Grand Historian Lu Zhi inscribed his portrait, saying:
"The tiger has no teeth; the dragon does not roar. The moon is dark over a thousand forests; the six directions are shrouded in clouds. The distant mountains..."
Drawing eyebrows, with cheeks like red apricots, she marries the spring breeze without a matchmaker.
Even a housewife in her thirty-fifth year knows how to apply rouge and powder here and there.

(From the *Yinshan ji*) Dharma Master Zhengwu Zhi was the son of the Lin family of Tiantai. From his youth he was intelligent; he could recite from memory any book after reading it once. Although he was a physician...
He was also thoroughly proficient in divination and the interpretation of omens. One day, while visiting a lecture hall, he heard a discourse on the *Amitābha Sūtra*.
Listening intently for a long time, he sighed and said, "The place where the sun sets is my native land; hearing this today is like receiving a letter from home.

Thereupon, he shaved his head and vowed to diligently propagate the ancestral teachings. He relied upon Master Bai-lian Xian to inquire about the Way of complete transformation. Master Xian pointed to a lantern.

He said: "To be detached from nature and cut off from non-existence is, by its very essence, originally empty and quiescent; thus the principle is complete. Yet, because the perceptions of the six classes of ordinary beings and the four types of noble ones differ, transformation remains present.
When wisdom does not accord [with reality], one subsequently attains awakening through causes. Once, while sweeping the floor and reciting the *Lotus Sūtra*, he reached the passage:

'Know that dharmas are eternally without nature; the Buddha-seed arises from conditions. His mind then suddenly opened up in clear realization. Xuanshan saw him and said: 'I am glad that this great matter has been accomplished.'"

[The teaching of] the *Lotus Sūtra* is decisively settled; this [text on] *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* serves as its vital core. You have been able to achieve awakening and truly penetrate the subtle and the wondrous.
Since then, you have allowed your mind to roam in clarity and vastness, frequently demonstrating this to others. Every five days, you would finally sleep for a single night;

at all other times, you immersed yourself in the essentials of the Way, fearing only that you might not go far enough. You sat upon Mount Dong for twenty-four years, and the disciples from both mountains...
In his debates, no one dared to oppose him. The Master once lamented that later generations were confined within the fetters of names and marks (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*), clinging to their records;
some even treat the transmission of an entire school as a mere study of texts. Other schools look down upon this with disdain, failing to grasp its essence.
Consequently, he exhorted his disciples, saying: "Do you not reflect on what our Buddha said? 'This is true diligence. In these very words alone, there is [the entirety of the teaching]."
Regarding the karmic conditions for those of superior capacity: why not directly stimulate and clarify this matter?
Later, when he was commissioned to go to Upper Zhushan, Prime Minister Qin asked, "Are the methods of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) one dharma or two dharmas?

The Master replied, "They are one dharma. It is like water: that which is still and clear is *śamatha*; that which can reflect one's beard and hair is *vipaśyanā*. The water is but one. Furthermore, it is also like...

It is like military force; it is employed only when there is no other choice. Taking the maladies of sentient beings—profound ignorance and vast distraction—as the illness, one employs the medicine of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) to rescue their mind-nature, returning it to its state as a single, perfect essence, so that the Dharma-realm becomes tranquil. This tranquility is called *śamatha*.

That which is tranquil yet constantly illuminating is called *vipaśyanā*. If one were to focus exclusively on what is above [the head], what would there be to observe? It would be like a high official wearing his ceremonial sash and holding his upright jade tablet.
Sitting in meditation within the ancestral temple, he restored the realm without raising a weapon; it was simply a matter of this.
The Master said with joy, "Were it not for you, how could I have known the subtlety of the Buddha-dharma?

(From the Stele Inscription) Dongshan Nengxing was a man of practice whose teachings and contemplation were clear and lucid; he took cultivation as his primary resolve, and once he entered the hall of repentance, [he remained there] regardless of cold or heat.
He remained unchanged for forty years. Consequently, the reputation of this practitioner spread throughout Jiang and Zhejiang. Yet Zhen'e never once claimed to be a practitioner;
he would simply say, "The Master Zhì (Zhiyi) performed the six periods of prostrations to the Buddha and sat in meditation during four periods;
these are the standard rituals of practice. How could I possibly possess such qualities? Master Cān'ān once sat with him in close proximity while practicing together.

He was observed to be upright, neither lax nor biased. Whenever he fell ill, he would simply abstain from food for several days without ceasing his meditation or recitation, and his illness would heal on its own.
He was naturally firm and pure, loathing fame and profit; whatever offerings he received, he immediately distributed among the community without retaining even a hair’s breadth.
All he possessed were tattered robes and worn-out rags. In summer, he used bamboo strips...
He bound them together as rafters and eaves; in winter, he took them to ward off the cold. Whenever he entered the mountains to feed tigers, the tigers harbored no intent to harm him.
Or, during wind and rain on dark nights, he would sit in meditative repose upon mounds and tombs; his body and mind remained tranquil, free from any fear.

The mountain deity of the monastery manifested spiritual transformations throughout the region and was constantly accessible to him. When the provisions from the Fragrant Accumulation Hall (Gandhakuṭī) were insufficient, the administrative officials would invariably report the matter to Neng, who—

He immediately offered a prayer. On the following day, the donor arrived, filling the doorway. When the monk asked the reason for his visit, the donor replied, "Last night, as I was making my rounds, I was told that the monastery’s provisions were exhausted;
I have come specifically to offer this support. (From the *Xingzhuang*) Chan Master Fenyang Wuye Zhaowu was a native of Taiyuan.
His character and insight were profound and deep, and he was naturally free from artifice in his youth. He possessed great ambition. Regarding one [matter]...
He mastered all written characters naturally, without relying on the instruction of a teacher. Orphaned at a young age, he grew weary of the world and left the household life.

He studied under more than seventy renowned masters, from all of whom he perfectly grasped their respective lineages. He stayed briefly wherever he went and took no pleasure in sightseeing; some even criticized him for lacking aesthetic refinement.
Baoshou Zhao sighed and said, "My late master traveled on foot precisely because his sacred mind had not yet attained full penetration; he hurried about to seek definitive discernment."
"Is it not for the sake of enjoying the sights of mountains and waters? Later, he visited Shoushan and asked about the meaning of the phrase "rolling up the mat.

Shoushan said, "When the dragon’s sleeve is swept aside, its whole body is revealed. Zhao asked, "What is your own intention, Master? [Shoushan replied,] "Where the Elephant King walks, there is no trace of foxes.
Zhao then attained great enlightenment and said: "The moon in the empty expanse of the ten-thousand-year-old azure pool—only after repeated and weary straining does it finally respond."
He understood. He prostrated and returned to the assembly. At that time, Master Xing of Ye County was serving as the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera).
He asked, "What principle have you realized that you are so self-accepting? Zhao replied, "This is precisely where I let go of my body and life.

Later, Zhang Gong, the Prefectural Governor of Changsha, invited Zhao to choose among four famous monasteries to reside in. Zhao said, "I am merely a monk who constantly walks for alms; I am one who transmits the Buddha-mind."

The position of *shō* (abbot) is no minor office. Although he was invited eight times in succession, he steadfastly did not respond. Later, when he was welcomed by the Imperial Prince’s Academy, he closed his door and lay high in bed.
Zen Master Shimon Sō entered by forcing open the door and reproached him, saying, "The Great Matter of the Buddha-Dharma is more important than the minor detail of retiring in peace.
You are one with the power to shoulder the Great Dharma; at such a time as this, why do you wish to sleep soundly? Thus, [Kōshō]...
Startled, he rose and said, "If it were not for you, I would never have heard such words. Prepare my things at once; I am going.

Upon arriving, he sat in meditation upon a single mat, his shadow never leaving the mountain for thirty years. The Master, concerned that the cold in Fenzhou was too severe, wished to discontinue the night assemblies.
He was moved by the request for the Dharma made by a strange bhikṣu. Li Gong, the Prefect of Longde Fu, sent him three times to welcome him at Chengtian;
yet he did not go. The messenger was due to be punished. He came again and said, "I must have you, Master, to go with me; otherwise there will be punishment."
The Master said, "You should keep this in mind. Zhaor said, "One must distinguish between priority and sequence; why must they be simultaneous?
Zhaor ordered that provisions be prepared and urged him to pack his belongings, saying, "I am going. He set down his chopsticks and passed away.
(From the *Sengbao zhuan*) The Real Man Zhang Pingshu was naturally fond of the pure and the void. While in the marketplace of Danqiu, he encountered Ding Rupi. [He] came forth...

He then grasped the significance of the number borne by the dragon horse. After a long time, his practice was perfected, and he remarked, "Though my physical form is firm, I have never yet investigated the nature of primordial enlightenment.
He subsequently explored the Buddhist scriptures (*nèi-diǎn*). Upon reaching the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he attained a profound realization and composed the *Wùzhēn Piān* (Treatise on Awakening to Truth).
He also wrote songs and hymns of the Chan school; in the preface to one of these, he cited the ten kinds of immortals from the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, whose lifespans last for ten million years.
It is said that those who do not cultivate correct awakening will, when their retribution is exhausted, be reborn and scattered into the various realms of existence.

Furthermore, it says: "One who pursues this Way should take the Great Void as the essence of the mind, such that the internal and external are as one. If even a single speck of dust is established, it immediately becomes a leakage.

This is a subtle excellence that cannot be transmitted through words. If one understands the *Vajracchedikā Sūtra* and the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, the meaning of the Golden Elixir (*Jindan*) will become clear of itself. Why?

One must certainly distinguish between the differences and similarities of Laozi and Śākyamuni. Thus we know that Pingshu (Wang Bi) sought the dharma for escaping birth and death, and that he ultimately relied upon the Buddha as his final refuge. (From *Qunxian Zhuyu*):
The Perfected Man Lü Dongbin was a native of Heyang. He was born during the Tianbao era of the Tang dynasty; his family had served as prominent officials for generations.

Having failed to pass the jinshi examinations despite multiple attempts, he traveled to Mount Hua where he met Zhongli Quan. Zhongli Quan was a former general of the Jin dynasty who had fled the chaos to study the methods for nourishing life;
he intended to transmit these teachings to Lü Gong, whom he first tested by giving him wealth as alms.

One day, while traveling with Lü Gong, Zhongli Quan picked up a piece of stone and smeared it with medicine, whereupon it immediately turned into gold. Zhongli Quan gave it to him, saying, "You shall use this to buy gruel on the road ahead."
Lü asked, "Will this still be destroyed? Zhong replied, "It will be destroyed in five hundred years. Lü threw it down, saying, "In the future, it might mislead others.
Zhong then tested him again by means of his appearance, commanding Lü to enter the mountains to gather medicinal herbs.

He transformed into a small cottage where a beautiful woman welcomed him joyfully, saying, "My husband has been gone for a long time; now that I have met you, a gentleman, I pray you do not abandon me. The woman desired—
He took his hand and drew near. Lü pushed him away with his hand, saying, "Do not defile me with this leather bag.

As soon as he had finished speaking, the woman vanished; she was none other than Zhongli. Thereupon, [Lü Dongbin] was granted the art of the Golden Elixir and the methods of the Celestial Immortal Sword.
He subsequently attained the ability to travel at will. A poem says: "Morning I roam in Nan Yue, evening in Cangwu; A green serpent is hidden within my sleeve."

His temperament was coarse and bold; for three days he remained unrecognized by the people of Yueyang. He chanted aloud as he flew over Lake Dongting and went to visit Master Longya to inquire about the essential meaning of the Buddha-dharma.
Longya gave him this verse: "For what reason do you grieve at dawn and grieve at dusk?

If one does not learn in youth, one will feel shame in old age. It is not that the bright pearl is cherished by the black dragon; It is simply that people of this age do not know how to seek it. Because of this...
Passing by Mount Huanglong in Ezhou, he saw purple qi swirling about and suspected that a person of extraordinary character was staying there.

He entered the monastery and encountered Chan Master Ji ascending the hall to teach. Master Ji, knowing there was an extraordinary person hidden among the assembly, sat down and then said in a stern voice, "There is someone in the crowd who is secretly seeking the Dharma.
Lu Yi then boldly asked, "A single grain of millet contains a world; within half a pint of a cauldron, one boils the universe."
"Shanzhou," [the Master said]. "Tell me, how is this principle? The Master replied, "A corpse-guarding ghost. Lü said, "But what can be done?
There is the elixir of longevity and immortality within my bag. The Master said, "Even if it endures eighty thousand kalpas, it will ultimately fall into emptiness and oblivion.
Lü departed in indignation. That night, he flew with his sword to threaten him. The Master had already foreseen this; he covered his head with his dharma robe and sat there.
The Master [Baizhang] brandished his sword, circling it several times around him. The Master pointed at it with his finger, and the sword immediately fell to the ground.

Lü apologized for his transgression. The Master then interrogated him, saying: "I shall not ask about the half-measure cooking pot; how is it that 'within a single grain of millet, the world is concealed'?
At these words, Lü attained realization. He then composed a verse, saying: "I have snapped the ladle and smashed the zither; now I no longer harbor attachments."
Gold in the Water. Since seeing Huanglong for the first time, I have finally realized that all my previous efforts were based on a mistaken application of the mind.
(From *Xianyuan yishi*) The layman Feng Jie, a Court Gentleman, traveled as a youth to the Imperial Academy. One day, he was tested with the essay topic "The Virtue of the Living is Radiant.
He won first place; his composition elucidated the meaning of the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra*. Although he remained on the path of official service, he did not forget [his spiritual practice].

Regarding his Buddhist studies: he traveled extensively to consult renowned masters. While residing at Longmen, as Fuyan was walking in meditation, a young boy happened to run across the courtyard reciting:
"Amidst the myriad phenomena, the body alone is revealed. Fuyan patted the boy on the back and said, "Excellent! At that moment, [Foguo] attained realization.

Later, while serving as the military governor of Lunan, he often sat in meditative seclusion; whenever he had leisure from public affairs, he delighted in sitting in *dhyāna*. Previously, he had once...
The phrase "reclining on the bed with arms crossed" [refers to his practice], yet he applied himself even more earnestly to the Pure Land practices (*śukla-karma*).

Wherever he went, he established assemblies for the cultivation of mindfulness (*smṛti-bhāvanā*) to exhort both the clergy and the laity. Since the outbreak of war, the Buddhist canon had been reduced to ashes; rather than seeking personal enrichment, he dedicated all his stipends exclusively to the restoration of the Tripitaka.
There is a verse that briefly says: "I am afflicted by a chronic obsession; though I possess wealth, it remains empty and void. I make no plans for descendants."
It was not spent on carriages or horses, nor used for luxuries or fine living, nor purchased for the pleasures of sound and sight.

Without a single awl to buy southern fields, and without a single tile to build a house, the monthly stipend received was used solely to redeem Buddhist scriptures, so that those who open and read them might [attain liberation].
All may enter the realm of Nirvana without remainder. For the sake of a half-verse, ancient Buddhas even sacrificed their entire bodies.

Therefore, do not begrudge your wealth, but reveal the truth to all deluded followers. Ask those who cling to riches: they spend their days weighing every grain of dust, yet when impermanence suddenly arrives upon this earth, [they find nothing].

"Can one truly escape birth and death? In the twenty-third year of the Xiangshu era, when the Master was governing Changsha, news suddenly arrived that a close acquaintance had set the date for his passing on the third day of the seventh month.
On that day, he ordered a high seat to be prepared in the rear hall and received guests as he normally did.
Descending the steps, he gazed toward the palace gate and performed a solemn prostration. He requested that the Canal Commissioner take charge of the prefectural affairs.

Donning his monastic robes and sandals, he sat upon a high seat and exhorted all officials, clerks, and both monastics and laypeople to advance on the Path and support the teachings of the Dharma-gate.
Thereupon, he took up his staff, rested it against his knee, and passed away. (From the epitaph by Man Dapin)
When Zhao Qingxian Gong was over forty years old, he had set aside the sounds and colors of the secular world to seek the ancestral Way.
He encountered Chan Master Fohui Quan, who was residing at Nanchan Temple in Quzhou; the Gong visited him daily. Quan never permitted him to utter a single erroneous word.

Later, while serving as the Governor of Qingzhou, amidst his administrative duties, he devoted much time to Chan meditation and discourse. Suddenly, during a great and startling peal of thunder, he attained a sudden realization. He composed this verse:
He said: "Sitting silently in the public hall, leaning back with hands folded upon the desk; the source of the mind is unmoving, as still as water.
With a single clap of thunder, the crown of the head opens, awakening that which was one's own from before. Upon hearing this, Quan remarked, "Zhao Yuedao has merely struck lucky.
(From the *Meixi ji*)
Chan Master Jì of Yangshan was the son of the Ye family in Shaozhou. After shaving his head, he dreamed that he obtained a large pearl whose radiance pierced people.
Upon waking, he said, "This is the supreme jewel of the mind. Having obtained it, I shall clarify the ground of the mind. He then set out to travel.

Having visited Danyuan, he already attained an understanding of the profound essence. Later, upon meeting Guishan, he finally ascended to the inner sanctum. Guishan asked, "What is the dwelling place of the true Buddha?

Guishan replied, "By means of the wondrous state where thought is non-thought, one returns to the thought that is the inexhaustible spiritual flame. When thought is exhausted, one returns to the source;
nature and form are eternally present, and phenomena and principle are non-dual. The true Buddha is thusness. At these words, Huairang attained sudden enlightenment.

Having received the secret seal and leading the assembly, he resided at Wangmang Mountain. When his conditions for transforming others were not yet harmonized, he traveled to Yuanzhou to visit Yangshan.

As he went upstream along the river, two deities met him and asked, "This deep mountain is utterly perilous; from where have you come, Master? The Master replied, "I wish to seek a site for a hermitage.
The deities said, "It is by our own merit and fortune that we have encountered you. We pray that you grant us this mountain to you, Master."

As for his dwelling, the Master said, "Since you have bestowed this upon me, I must possess a vast and expansive mind; only when I no longer perceive the faults of the monks shall I accept your gift. The deity replied, "So be it.
The deity then pointed to the base of Mount Jiyun and said, "Do not dwell elsewhere than here. The Master thereupon tied up a thatched hut and resided there.
He lived on wild fruits and drank from mountain streams, sitting upright throughout the entire day. Before long, the two deities appeared and said, "Disciples..."

As they were about to move it, the disciples found their dwelling place inconvenient and decided they should relocate it. When night fell, wind and thunder suddenly broke out in a storm. They moved the temple thirty *li* to Dutián;
the ancient clay statues of the deities and the giant pine trees all followed along. This was the fourth month of summer in the third year of the Huichang era.
A strange monk arrived from the sky, saying: "I have come specifically to the Eastern Land to pay homage to Mañjuśrī. Today, however—"

He encountered the minor Śākyamuni. From that time on, the spiritual style of the Mí-yáng lineage flourished greatly in the world. As the Master was about to pass into *parinirvāṇa*, a deity sought his final words.
The Master said, "This body of mine, like a phantom or a bubble, arises and passes away according to conditions. When it came, there was nothing; when it departs, what more is there to seek?
The deity said, "When the various Buddhas entered extinction, devas and nāgas requested their final instructions. I pray you do not disregard me. The Master, regarding the Dharma he had attained—

The Master, Chan Master You of Mount Guishan, had entrusted [this matter] for the memorial vegetarian feast on the eighth day of the first month; until the present day, the common people have dared not disobey it.

(From the Temple Records) Dharma Master Dao was a native of Shunchang in the Western Capital. During the Xuanhe era, he was summoned by imperial decree to be converted into a "De-shi" (Virtuous Man). The Master opposed Lin Lingsu.
He debated the heterodox and the orthodox, appealing his case to the imperial court. Having incurred the Emperor’s displeasure, he was exiled to serve as a prison supervisor in Daozhou.

The guardsman said, "The journey ahead is ten thousand *li*; you ought to consume meat and wine to bolster your physical strength. The Master replied, "Death is the mandate of Heaven; it is forbidden by the Buddha and I may not transgress it.
The guardsman then respectfully submitted to the Master. One day before arriving at his place of exile, the Prefect dreamed at night that a Buddhist image entered the city wearing a cangue.

The city officials also had the same dream. The following morning, when the Master arrived, the Great Governor said to those around him, "This monk who has been punished must surely be an extraordinary person.
Before even a month had passed, more than half of the people in the district fell ill. The Master dug a pond and consecrated its waters with prayers.
Those who drank were all healed. Thus, the people of that region revered him as nothing less than a father or a teacher. Soon after, he was ordered to travel by way of Changsha;
there he met Jiyin, who sent him a poem saying: "Master Dao’s courage exceeds his physical frame;
He dares to write a remonstrance against the scales of the dragon. Desiring only to bare his shoulders and bear the Buddha-dharma, He willingly extends his neck to receive the axe. 3.
Though exiled for many years, his heart remained free of shame; returning from ten thousand *li*, his countenance showed no signs of withering.
Recently, it was heard that he had donned his ceremonial boots and tablets to attend court.

At that time, the high officials and great ministers, recognizing that the Master possessed both civil and military talent, requested that he be granted a cap and robe, invested with official rank, and entrusted with military command to recover the lost territories. The Master declined these honors with all his might, and the court nobles took note of this.
His resolve could not be shaken. He submitted a petition requesting the bestowal of the title Baojue Yuantong Fajie (Precious Enlightenment, Perfect Penetration, Dharma-Savior).
At the beginning of the Shaoxing era, he was summoned to the palace. The Emperor said, "The late Emperor was deluded by demonic arts and caused you to discard your monastic robes.

Would it be acceptable for Your Majesty and I to remove your branding and tattooing? The Master replied, "Though I am grateful for Your Majesty’s imperial grace, I cannot bear to erase the calligraphic legacy of the late Sovereign."
He destroyed it. The Emperor remarked, "This monk remains stubborn to the end; let him have his way.

In the third year of the Xiangshuo era, the Master and the Daoist Liu Ruqian went to the imperial court. Regarding their seating order at the site of the prayer ritual, the decree stated: [The decree is omitted as per instructions.]
During the Chongning era, Lin Lingsu and others shamelessly usurped official ranks and threw the imperial administration into disorder; consequently, the Daoist order eclipsed the Buddhist hierarchy.
Since the Jianyan era, all official titles and stipends held by Daoists have been rescinded.

As they no longer possess official patronage, we respectfully request that the Court issue a formal decree to restore the original regulations established by our ancestors and grant a special correction of this matter.
It was promulgated throughout the realm to rectify social customs; however, as state affairs were beset by many complications at the time, this proposal was temporarily set aside.
In the thirteenth year, the matter was re-examined and finalized: monks were established on the left and followers of heterodox paths on the right, which became a permanent regulation.

Later, when the drought demon caused great havoc, the Master was summoned by imperial decree to offer prayers. He immediately ascended the seat and offered his invocation, requesting four golden vases, each to be filled with fresh [water].
[He took] a carp, sprayed water upon it while reciting secret prayers, and immediately dispatched four swift-footed messengers to release it into the rivers and marshes.
Before the messengers had even returned, the rain had already poured down in torrents. The Emperor’s countenance was greatly pleased.
(From the Stele Inscription) Chan Master Huichan Guang was a native of Changle in Min. He crossed the mountain ridges to pay his respects to Yuanwu, Foxin, and other renowned masters.
Dahui was staying at Guangyin when Wuguan went to attend him. One day, while accompanying Dahui on a walk, Wuguan asked, "I have reached this point but cannot attain thorough penetration.
Where does my illness lie? Dahui said, "Your illness is most peculiar; even the world's physicians would fold their hands in helplessness. Why?
Because others die and cannot be revived, whereas you are now alive and have never died. You must reach the state of great peace and bliss."
"The field must undergo death once before it can be attained. Guangyi doubted this. Entering the room, he asked, "The congee has been eaten;
the bowl has been washed; the taboos have been removed. Now, bring forth a single phrase! Guang replied, "Torn asunder!

Hui Zhen let out a thunderous shout and said, "You are at it again, talking about Chan! At this, Guang attained great enlightenment. Hui beat the drum and announced to the assembly: "Rabbit’s hair..."
Seizing it, he laughs heartily. One blow opens ten thousand layers of gates and locks. What joy and fulfillment in life is found this very day!
Who says that a thousand miles have deceived me here? Guang presented this verse: A single pressure brings forth the roar of a thunderbolt at the critical moment;
It startles Mount Sumeru and causes the Northern Dipper to hide within it. The vast waves surge, flooding the heavens; Having seized the nostrils, one loses the mouth. (Verse)

The śramaṇa Puyao was a native of Goryeo. During the Kaihuang era, he went to Fulong to seek the dhyāna methods of Zhiyi. Before long, he attained realization.
Zhiyi said to him, "You have a karmic affinity with this; you ought to dwell in a secluded and quiet place to bring it to completion."
Practice sublime conduct. Today, six or seven *li* from the temple on Mount Huading in Tiantai is where I formerly practiced as a *dhūta*.
You should go there to study the Way and advance in your practice; there will surely be profound benefit. Do not worry about food or clothing.

Following the instructions of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, he went there and practiced the Way day and night without ever sleeping or lying down. For sixteen years, his shadow did not leave the mountain. One.

Zhengyan Chen Liaoweng was a native of Nanjian Prefecture. Having attained the highest degree in his youth, he was by nature refined and elegant, and lived in harmony with all things.

He was competitive [in his studies], yet when he saw the shortcomings of others, he never confronted them face-to-face; he would merely give a subtle hint to alert them. Initially, the Master still studied the *Avataṃsaka* (Huayan) school and attained considerable proficiency.

Later, when he encountered the Dharma Master Mingzhi and inquired about the fundamental tenets of Tiantai, Mingzhi showed him the "Inconceivable Realm" for those of superior faculties from the *Mohe Zhiguan*.

The question of "having a phrase" or "not having a phrase" is like a vine leaning against a tree; as soon as one opens their mouth, it is said to be not so.
One day, while Huì was taking medicinal food with a guest, he held the chopsticks in his hand but forgot to eat. Wù laughed and said to the guest, "This fellow has attained 'Huangyang Wood Zen.
Huì asked indignantly, "Did the Master not once ask the Fifth Patriarch about 'having a phrase' or 'not having a phrase'?"
"The phrase is like a vine leaning against a tree. How did the Patriarch answer? Wuzhuo said, "It cannot be described even by painting; it cannot be depicted even by drawing.
He asked again, "When the tree falls and the vine withers, where does the phrase return? The Patriarch said, "It comes along with you. Huizang raised his voice and said, "I understand!
From that moment on, he was suddenly enlightened and free from all obstructions. Not long after, he took the road toward Jiangxi and encountered [Master Baizhang].
Dai-zhi Han Zicang engaged in extensive discussions regarding Confucianism and Buddhism, and was profoundly moved by [the Master’s] teachings. He invited him to reside in his study for half a year.
Aside from exchanging greetings at the time of their morning rising, they were not permitted to discuss matters outside of that hour. In walking, they did not yield to one another in precedence;

in sitting, they did not inquire whether one was host or guest. They forgot themselves in mutual ease. Day after day, there was no teaching or dharma that did not bring them joy. Later, because of Chancellor Zhang Wei...
Dongshan invited him to take up residence at Mount Jing, where the monastics of the world followed him in droves. His assembly eventually numbered twenty thousand;
yet, rather than binding them with strict monastic regulations, he allowed them to govern themselves.

Whenever a Chan practitioner came to inquire about essential doctrines, or if their arguments were inconsistent or led to disputes before Dahui, Dahui would not adjudicate the matter, regardless of its magnitude or detail, but would invariably send the individual to the Hall Office to be expelled. At that time...
Weina Shaozhen was a man of righteousness from Shu. Whenever Dahui issued an order, Shaozhen would suppress it and refuse to carry it out;

at worst, he would suggest that Dahui go on a mountain tour. Later, when Dahui heard of this, he praised him greatly, saying, "How could there be such a *yuèzhòng* (a monk who manages communal affairs) outside the Dragon Elephant Grotto of Miaoxi?
Ying Zhongwen remarked, "It is because the Master is magnanimous and values righteousness, possessing a lofty understanding and a noble character."
Though he was urgent, his judgment was truly broad; though he was amidst anger and abuse, he was truly compassionate.

When there were those among the assembly who did not comply with the Vinaya, he would at once act according to the regulations, never having harbored the slightest intention to harm people or damage things. That the Master praised him so deeply must have had profound significance.
Should not later generations take this as a mirror? (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks)
Chan Master Yezhu Chuan was a member of the *gongji* (militia) in Su. Because of seeds planted in previous lives, he delighted in hearing the Dharma of Chan.

He frequently attended upon Chan Master Jian of Jingde Temple. When Jian showed him the kōan concerning Zhaozhou’s “The dog has no Buddha-nature,” he investigated it day and night, to the point that he neglected his official duties.
The magistrate, enraged, flogged him. Suddenly, beneath the blows of the staff, he attained great enlightenment regarding the profound essentials. Jian then changed [his name].

His name was [Chuan]; you formerly called him Diksan. Your name is Daochuan. From now on, if you can straighten your backbone and exert yourself even more, then your path will increase like the swelling of a river;
if you are negligent, there is no need to speak of it. Chuan received these instructions with reverence, and his resolve never wavered.
He once chanted the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, which is practiced in the world today. He established the Dharma at Yefu during the winter.
Upon reaching the point of addressing the assembly, he said: "The myriad shadows have vanished and the first yang has arisen; the grasses, trees, gardens, and groves all sprout their buds.
Only the bottomless bowl of the patch-robed monk remains as before, holding both rice and soup.
(From the *Zhufeng ji*) Under the guidance of Chan Master Deshan Xuanmi, there was a practitioner who applied himself with great intensity, contemplating the "dog has no Buddha-nature" koan.
The practitioner had long been unable to penetrate the nature of the teaching. One day, he suddenly saw a dog’s head as large as the sun’s orb, opening its mouth as if to devour him.
Terrified, the practitioner rose from his seat and fled. When a neighbor asked the reason for this, the practitioner related the incident in detail and went to report it to Deshan.
Deshan said, "There is no need to fear. Simply exert your full mental acuity and, as soon as it opens its mouth, dash inside."

Having granted permission, he departed. The Chan practitioner sat according to the instructions until midnight. When the dog appeared again as before, the practitioner struck it with his head with all his might, whereupon it was found inside a chest.
Thereupon, he attained sudden enlightenment. Later, he appeared in the world as Wenshu, whose Dharma teachings flourished greatly;
he was none other than Master Zhen. (From the *Meixi Bilu*)
Shen Zhao asked Master Fazhi, "What is the King of Sutras? The Master replied, "You have served as my steward for the storehouse for three years;
after that, I shall tell you. Shenru respectfully accepted this command. When the three years were complete, Shenru requested again, saying, "Now you should speak.
The Master shouted once, "Benru! Suddenly, Shenru attained realization and composed a verse: [Verse omitted per instructions]
It is said: "Everywhere one meets the path home; at every turn is one's native land. Since this is a matter already accomplished from the beginning, why wait for deliberation?

(From the *Jiaoxinglu*). Dharma Master Chaa Yan attained ordination by passing the scriptural examinations and relied upon Shenzhao of Dongshan. Shenzhao, recognizing his capacity, said: "Our school..."
He gained the support of others so that the Dharma would not decline. He was promoted to the foremost position among his peers. The Master did not merely regard lecturing as paramount;

rather, whether in matters of conduct or silence, he ensured they were always in accord with the Dharma before ceasing. At that time, Fazhen asked about the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*) of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
The Master replied: "The myriad dharmas are but the one mind; outside the mind there are no separate dharmas. Since neither mind nor dharmas can be apprehended, this is [the inconceivable realm]."
He was named Miaosanqian. Not long after, Fazhen moved to Dongye. When Fazhen retired from his duties, he commanded the Master to succeed him.
The Master said, "In the past, when Zhizhe was not yet fifty, he dispersed his disciples. At forty-four, he reached the age of forty and sat perpetually without lying down.
I am now old; who else am I? How could I find the leisure to dwell in the mountains? Ultimately, he did not accept the offer and lived in seclusion at Lingjiu.

On the Eastern Peak, there was a single *jia* (quince) tree. I built a hermitage beside it and named it the Jia Hermitage. The inscription reads: "At the age of sixty, I returned to seek a thatched hut.
Once the hermitage was completed, I stayed within it to recuperate from illness; furthermore, I did not intend to adopt eccentricity to stir the common world.
To the left of the hermitage stood a single *jia* tree, and thus it was named. Now, the *jia* is neither a famous fruit nor a rarity; compared to it—"
How could the pear and the chestnut not feel shame? Yet the pear is carved because of its crispness; the chestnut is eaten because of its sweetness.
Even if the pear and chestnut possessed consciousness and sought for themselves a place of uselessness, it would still be impossible to attain.
As for that *zhā* fruit, it is of the same class as the *pó*; though fragrant, it is astringent. One may force oneself to eat it, but the fragrance cannot fill the belly, and its astringency remains.
One must not allow the palate to grow weary; even a mere child of three feet might rarely find anything to pluck here.
These stones lie piled upon the branches in a state of self-satisfaction—this is indeed admirable. Alas! Man toils his bones because of his intelligence;
the jujube fruit remains secure in its place because of its astringency. Intelligence? Astringency? Which is the true? I, lacking intelligence, have found myself a neighbor to the jujube. Master.
He possessed only a single small alms bowl as his personal requisite; for his morning and midday meals, he took only the "three whites.

Thus he lived alone for twenty years, sitting in meditation with his door closed, beyond the reach of worldly intimacy. He observed the precepts of the *Vinaya* with equal care regarding both minor and major rules.

Even the most trivial items he used, down to the wooden wedges for his hearth, were kept with meticulous purity. Finding self-contentment in solitude, he devoted himself solely to the practice of *An-yang* (Pure Land).
As he was awaiting this, one night he dreamed that a great lotus flower grew from the middle of a pond, surrounded by four rows of celestial music.
The Master said, "This is the sign of my Pure Land. Seven days later, he indeed passed away.

(*Gyōgyō-tōki*) Formerly, there was an elder who was held in high esteem by his religious community for his mastery of the Way. In his later years, he received an imperial decree to reside at a mountain monastery.
Yajia was highly honored by the sagely sovereign. At the time of his death, the Emperor was deeply grieved and issued an imperial decree for his funeral procession.

A court attendant reported that this monk’s robes and alms-bowl were excessively wealthy, leading to complaints from the authorities; the Emperor was displeased, and his favor and respect consequently declined.
Shaoyun said, "What a pity! Worldly gain can obscure one's reputation and ruin one's virtue. How can those who possess abundant stores and receive heavy offerings not be cautious?"

Precepts. (From the *Shaoyun Zapi*) An ancient virtuous master spoke this verse to the assembly at the bathhouse: "From the beginning, this body is foul-smelling and a false composite; skin, hair, and oily secretions arise with every passing moment.
Even if one were to empty the oceans and wash all day long, one would not attain purity until the year of the donkey. The body is besmeared with dust and grime."
The wine is still shallow, yet the mind’s defilement by the objects of desire is even deeper. How pitiable are those throughout the world who have forgotten their source;
they cleanse only the skin and do not wash the heart. Filling a bushel with hot water and pouring it with a large ladle, the donor further hopes for reciprocal benefit.
If future generations do not know where [the merit] comes from, their blessings will vanish as quickly as Mount Sumeru melts away. (Inscribed on a stone at Lake Heart)

Fen’an Zhu was so fiercely dedicated to the Way that he had no leisure for food or rest. One day, leaning against a stone railing while contemplating the "dog" koan, he did not notice the rain falling until his clothes were soaked;
only then did he realize it was raining. Later, while walking along the riverbank, he heard the attendant shout, "The Senior Secretary is coming!
and suddenly attained great enlightenment. His verse says: "For many years this matter has hung in my breast. I have questioned all the masters..."

The square pupils did not open; at that moment, his liver and gallbladder were both rent asunder. With a single cry, "The Minister of the River has arrived," he thereafter ceased to dwell in fixed abodes.
He lived in a hermitage at Jianmen, and his transformative influence spread beyond the Ling region. His gāthās were composed with a swift brush. He inscribed his own portrait, saying:
"His features are coarse and searching; his speech is thin and vile. He is dazed and intoxicated, yet磊磊落落 (leileiluo) [lofty and unencumbered]. He scolds the wind..."
"Scolding the rain, one should be compassionate; whether they be sage or commoner is difficult to discern. Every day at the head and tail of the bridge, he waits for that person.
Without a Wang Liang or Bo Le, a lifetime passes in vain.
(Yinyan) Chan Master Lingyuan Qing was a native of Wuning in the Southland. His spirit was crystalline and clear, and he was tireless in his pursuit of learning. Huang Tai...
The History says: Master Qing was so devoted to learning that he was like one who craves food and drink out of hunger and thirst.

Relying on Master Huìtáng, he investigated and resolved his doubts day and night to the point of forgetting to sleep or eat. One day, while Huìtáng was conversing with a guest and Master Qing was standing in attendance, the guest departed and a long time passed;
yet Qing remained standing in his original place. Huìtáng called out to him, saying, "Brother Qing, you have died! At these words, he attained enlightenment.

Qing wrote in a letter to Fojian: "In my capacity as abbot of two monasteries, whenever I receive letters from my elder brother, Master Dongshan, there has never been a single word concerning worldly affairs.
His earnest instructions and entrustments concern nothing other than casting aside one's body to propagate this Way.
Upon arriving at Huanglong, he received a letter stating: "This year all the manors have suffered from drought damage; I do not worry about those at all, but I only worry..."
The Chan school has lost its eye. During one summer retreat, more than a hundred people entered the room to contemplate the "Vzhou’s Dog" koan, yet not a single person could penetrate it;

this is truly cause for concern. How profound these words! They stand in stark contrast to those who worry that their monasteries lack the means to avoid the resentment of officials, or who fear that their reputations will not spread and their followers will not flourish—such people are far removed from the true reality (as recorded in the *Tingjiang Biyu* and other texts).
Chan Master Fodeng Xun was a native of Xiachuan. For a long time he relied upon Master Foguan, following the assembly in requesting instruction, yet he made no progress whatsoever.
Suddenly he sighed and said, "If I do not attain thorough realization in this life, I vow never again to spread my bedding.
Thereupon, for forty-nine days, he relied solely on a pillar, standing as if he had lost his parents. Coincidentally, Foguan ascended the hall and said: "The dense..."
From the heavens and earth down to the myriad phenomena, all are sealed by this single Dharma. Xu then attained sudden enlightenment and went to see Foguan.
Foguan said, "What a pity that this bright pearl has been picked up by such a madman. When Yuanwu heard of this, he doubted it was not so.
He said, "I must test him before I can grant my realization. He sent someone to summon him. While wandering through the mountains, they happened upon a mountain pond.
Huineng pushed Wuxue into the water and immediately asked, "Before Niutou saw the Fourth Patriarch, what was it like? Wuxue, flustered, replied, "The pond is deep; the fish gather there.
He asked again, "After he saw him, what was it like? "The tree is high; it beckons the wind. He asked once more, "What about seeing and..."

When asked, "How was it before you had seen [the truth]? he replied, "Stretching out one's legs while they are still within the folded ones. Daewon praised him for this (from the *Jufeng Yulu* and other records).

Master Xian of Xiuzhou was five years old when his refined and elegant spirit already shone brightly; his mother marveled at him and sent him to Zisheng Monastery to become a monk. After traveling through various Chan assemblies, he returned;
however, there was no Chan residence in the Xiuzhou region to accommodate those who came seeking the Way. Furthermore, there was... (text fragmentary).

[The text is] missing. The Master then reorganized his monastery according to the rules for Chan masters of the ten directions. At that time, the monastic community in the region of Wu had lost its order;
they arbitrarily relied on high status and power, and no longer discussed matters based on precepts or virtue.

The Master was indignant and once petitioned the authorities with a letter to rectify the situation, successfully restoring the proper order of affairs. The Master said to Mingjiao Song: "I am unable to bestow the Great Benevolence through the Way."

Regarding material things, your virtuous conduct is further insufficient to be admired, which brings shame upon the former sages. If you merely endure to witness the corruption of the Dharma, this only increases your shame.
Mingjiao said: "There is no need for such humility. The wondrous path of the School of the Patriarchs is rarely reached;

the twelve dhūtas are the transcendent practices of those who have left the world. These are what our followers find difficult. To strive for the sake of the Dharma while disregarding one's own person—"

That which is difficult for others to achieve, Master [Yuanzhao] was able to practice. How, then, could he feel any shame? (From the *Inscription on the Shadow Hall*) Chan Master Yuanzhao Ben was a native of Changzhou.
His natural character was pure and refined, requiring no artificial adornment. He relied upon Master Tianyi Huai;

wearing tattered clothes and with a soiled face, he helped manage the well and mortar, and attended to the cooking and stoves. By day, he busied himself with monastic affairs; by night, he... [text continues].

He sat in meditation until dawn, applying himself with such diligent and arduous effort that he never slackened for even a moment. Someone said to him, "The dhūta ascetic bears the burden of the assembly;
you are truly weary. Puji replied, "If one abandons even a single dharma, one cannot be called fulfilled. I am determined to realize bodhi through bodily witness in this very life."
"How could I dare speak of weariness? Thus, Shuiguang left his seat vacant and appointed the Master to preside over it. Upon his arrival, he struck the drum to assemble the congregation;
suddenly, the drum fell to the ground, spinning and emitting a thunderous resonance. A monk called out, "This is an auspicious omen that this Master’s Dharma-thunder shall shake the earth.
In an instant, the monk vanished. From then on, the Dharma assembly flourished greatly. Later, as various monasteries vied to welcome him, [the Master] passed away in his later years.

Master Jingci was close friends with Vinaya Master Lingzhi Zhao. Zhao bestowed upon him his Dharma robes; throughout his life, whenever the Master ascended the seat for formal preaching, he invariably wore these robes.
While in meditative absorption, Dharma Master Xi of the Eastern Capital saw the lotus flowers of the Pure Land inscribed with large golden characters that read:
"The Bhikṣu Zongben sits at Yongming Temple in Hangzhou. Xi marveled at this occurrence and went specifically to pay his respects.
He asked, "Master, you belong to the school of the Separate Transmission (Biezhuan). How can there be a place for the Pure Land?
He replied, "Although I am within the Chan gate, I always cultivate the Pure Land concurrently.

(From the *Xingye dengji*). Chan Master Yangshan Yuan was a native of Yuyang. After receiving the precepts, he was courageous and resolute in his pursuit of the Way. Hearing that Miaoxi resided at Mei...

Yang went to rely upon him, serving diligently in the kitchen and striving with rigorous austerity. Miaoxi, seeing that his capacity and insight were refined and keen, often regarded him as extraordinary.

Consequently, during a minor assembly (xiaocan), he heard [Miaoxi] cite Master Xiu’s saying: "An ordinary person possesses the dharmas of an ordinary person, yet the ordinary person does not know them."
He was fully endowed with the dharmas of the sages, yet the sages did not meet him. Had the sages met him, he would have been an ordinary person;
had an ordinary person known him, he would have been a sage. Suddenly there was a resonance between them. Later, he presided over Xiangfu and moved to Mount Yang at Yuan.
After seven days had passed since he took charge of affairs, he presided over the ceremony for the incense offering (*gaoxiang*) of the Chan Gate.

The head seat (*shouzuo*) led the assembly in a prostration, requesting instruction on the great matter of birth and death and the rapidity of impermanence, saying, "We humbly pray that you will compassionately reveal the causes and conditions.

Yuanxu replied, "If you wish to investigate and clarify the matter of birth and death, you must directly observe where birth comes from during the four postures of walking, standing, sitting, and reclining."
"From where does death come? Ultimately, what is the true face of birth and death? After a long silence, he did not rise from his seat;
he remained serene, like a cicada shedding its shell.

(From the *Xingzhuang*) Dahui said: "Among those who preside over the Dharma in recent times, none is equal to Zhenru Zhe. Among those who skillfully support the monastic community, none is equal to..."
Yangqi Hui was straightforward and sincere with Ciming; he was often negligent in his duties and had no sense of restraint.

Yangqi, however, forgot himself in serving him, fearing only that things might not be done thoroughly or that matters might not be accomplished. Even when braving the cold and the heat, he never once thought of his own comfort.
From Nan’uan until his death at Xinghua, for thirty years, he held the reins of discipline and governance throughout the entire life of Ciming.

This concludes the latter part. As for True Suchness (Tathatā): from the time he first began his travels as a wandering monk (*paryaṭaka*), until he entered the world to lead disciples, he forgot his own body for the sake of the Dharma, as if driven by nothing less than hunger and thirst.
Whether in moments of haste or amidst adversity, he showed no look of agitation nor spoke with hurried words.

His single room was serene and tranquil, where he found joy within himself. He once said: "If a patch-robed disciple lacks lofty insight and far-reaching vision within, and lacks a strict teacher or virtuous friend without, they will rarely [attain realization]."
That he was able to become a perfected vessel—how admirable! These two elders truly serve as an excellent model for future generations a thousand years hence.
(Letter to Xi Shan) Chan Master Shichuang Gong possessed a solitary and lofty spiritual practice and an abundance of intellectual acumen.

He long relied upon Chan Master Hongzhi of Tiantong, undergoing rigorous trials in every task, both great and small. One day, he returned to visit his mother, who said, "The purpose of your journey..."
"To save my parents from birth and death, I have long served as a ruler of men. If I do not clearly understand cause and effect, it will bring trouble upon me in the underworld.
Gong said, "I have not cheated the Sangha by even a hair’s breadth; even a single lamp flame was used with due distinction between self and others.
There is no need to worry about me. His mother said, "Even so, can one cross water without getting one's feet wet? (From the *Yiyun Lu*)
Mount Tai and Mount Hua may be leveled; food and drink may be dispensed with; yet filial piety must not be forgotten.

Thus, the great filial son is one who is equal to Heaven and Earth, concurrent with the Sun and Moon, and moves forward with vigor without ceasing. The great precept states: "Be filial and obedient to parents, teachers, and the Sangha.

Since filial piety is itself called the precept, how could filial piety be forgotten? For those of us who have shaved our heads and joined the ranks of the Triple Gem, regardless of whether we are poor—
Whether rich, noble, or lowly, one should value only the Way and value only filial piety.
If there are parents who have no relatives to support them, the Buddha permitted that one set aside a portion of one's robes and alms bowl to offer to them.
If one does not personally provide for the nourishment of one's parents, one is not a son of our Śākya. (From the *Conglin fenglun*)
Master Meng’an Pēng was a native of Jīnhuā in Wǔchǐ. Having encountered Master Chēxī Qīng, who had clarified the Great Matter, he successively presided over several great monasteries.
Students flocked to him from all directions, fearing they might be left behind. When the Master ascended the lecture hall to teach, he would not pre-read the commentaries.
He had his attendants record his every movement. With the *pratibhāna* of eloquence, he expounded the Dharma in an inexhaustible flow. He once said to the assembly:
"Since I began leading my disciples, I have lectured on the *Mohe zhiguan* (Mahā-śraddhotpāda-śāstra) seven times;

yet during the actual practice of cultivation, I have never uttered a single word. He further said: "Within this great treatise, I wish to raise a minor challenge, even one as small as a scrap of paper."
"It cannot be accomplished. This is because the nature of words is detached; all are liberation. Later, he presided over Yanqing Monastery in Mingzhou.
One day, while ascending the seat to lecture on the "Taming Husband" (the Buddha), several gentlemen suddenly arrived. As they listened to the Master’s chanting, the Master said:

If we discuss the affairs of a "great man" (zhūngfú) according to Confucianism, it is one who, like a loyal minister who does not fear death and a brave warrior who disregards life, is thus able to establish great undertakings for the world and achieve illustrious fame for ten billion generations;

even those who are not deluded or submerged by fame, profit, sound, or color are all called great men. If we speak according to our own teaching, however, it is by means of the threefold contemplation within a single mind that one becomes so.
The boat and rudder: using the fivefold repentance throughout the six periods of the day as oars and paddles, one subdues all demons and restrains all non-Buddhists;
this is what is called a "great man" (*mahāpuruṣa*). Thus the gentleman sighed in admiration and departed.

(Regarding his practice: Master Jiu Wuweiyu was a native of Yuyao. He received the essential meaning of the Dharma from Master Huijue Bi, and later traveled extensively through various Chan assemblies.

He once entered the quarters of Foji at Mount Jing. Foji would invariably summon the Master whenever he sat for meditation, commanding him to expound the essential tenets of the Tiantai school and the general meaning of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
He treated him with great favor. Upon leaving the world, the Master lived in pure cultivation, and students gathered like clouds.

Concerned that junior monks living in single rooms were becoming unrestrained, he expanded his residence into a communal hall, furnishing it with clean desks, bright windows, rush mats, and meditation boards. He swept it clean...

Nevertheless, there remained the tradition of ancient monastic communities. During lecture sessions, he observed scholars adhering rigidly to the literal text and contending with one another over divergent interpretations.
He sighed and said, "The Way of Tiantai flourished through Siming, yet it has also declined through Siming. Unless a sage were to be reborn, who could sustain it?
Those who understood him remarked that the Master spoke with true insight. By nature, the Master possessed keen intelligence, and his eloquence flowed like a stream.
His deportment was composed and graceful; he never came into conflict with others. Those who lived and traveled with him throughout his life never once saw him display an expression of joy or anger.

By day he would study the Seven Classics, and by night he would sit in meditative repose; this was his constant practice. He established the Wuwei Hermitage and retired there for the rest of his days. (Epitaph)
In the winter of the Guihai year of the Xiangshu era, Chan Master Dahui was granted imperial permission to return north.

At that time, the seat at Yuyang Monastery was vacant, and Master Hongzhi appointed Dahui as its abbot. Hongzhi had previously known that Dahui would bring many followers and that their food supplies would inevitably be exhausted;

thus, he informed the monastery administrators in advance, saying: "You must urgently prepare a large annual budget for me, and double the usual provisions required for the Hall of Fragrant Accumulation."
"Set it aside," he said. "The administrative affairs shall follow my instructions. The following year, Dahui indeed arrived, and the assembly numbered more than ten thousand.

Before long, Xiangji was exhausted of resources, and the multitude were all in a state of great anxiety. Dahui could not find a way to remedy it, so Hongzhi then distributed all his accumulated goods to assist them.
Consequently, the entire assembly received relief. Dahui went to express his gratitude, saying, "This is no ordinary Buddha."
"How could he possibly possess such power? One day, Dahui took Zhi's hand and said, "The two of us shall grow old together.
When you sing, I will join in; when I sing, you will join in. Should one of us suddenly pass away first, the survivor shall preside over the funeral rites.
A year later, Hongzhi passed away, and Dahui ultimately presided over the funeral, fulfilling his pledge. (From *Xuechuang zajì*)

Master Cíyuán was fully endowed with both realization and practice; scholars took him as their model. When the seat at Dongyè became vacant, the two masters Wén and Rán lit incense and requested the Master to preside over it.
Upon Cí’s arrival, the Dharma assembly flourished. During the height of summer, after the lecture concluded, he returned to his quarters to rest when Wén arrived.
Wén said to the Master, "The Dongyè monastic center has always had practitioners of the Way presiding over it, generation after generation."
After the lectures ended, he was either in the hall for repentance or in the meditation hall; he never once lay down to rest as he pleased.
When Ciman heard this, he said, "How could I dare not respect your command? From then on, whether in bitter cold or humid heat, he never slackened even slightly. (From the *Cān Lù*).
When National Teacher Nanyue Huairang visited the Sixth Patriarch, there was a prophecy by Prajñātāra which said: "Your branch of the Buddha-dharma..."
He departed from you; later, he appeared as a colt that trampled to death all the people in the world—this was none other than Mazu.

Mazu produced eighty-four *kalyāṇamitras* (spiritual friends), whom the people of the world called manifestations of Avalokiteśvara. Whenever they resided in monasteries, they were provided for by kings and ministers.
There was a monastery manager who oversaw the permanent assets for twenty years without keeping written records.
One day, when the officials conducted an audit of the accounts, he was imprisoned.
He then thought to himself, "I do not know whether this monk is an ordinary man or a sage; for twenty years I have assisted him, yet today I receive such bitter retribution.
Mazu became aware of this within the temple and instructed an attendant to prepare incense and enter meditative absorption with upright composure. At that moment, the warden of the prison suddenly—

His mind was opened; he recalled at once all the money and goods spent over twenty years, and had the scribe dictate and write them down as they were recounted, leaving nothing unaccounted for (*Tongming ji*).
Master Xuetang Xing said: "Gao'an was upright and vigorous in character; his movements and stillness were governed by method. Although he lived frugally himself,"

He was exceedingly generous toward others. Upon hearing that someone was ill, he regarded it as if it were his own. As for servants and laborers, he would personally go to visit and inquire after them, listening to whatever they required.
When they died, he did not ask whether their coffers were full or empty, but provided a full send-off according to the rites.
His profound compassion for all beings is truly an excellent model for this degenerate age. (Yiyun Lu)
In a letter from Imperial Historian Huang to Hu Shaobi, he wrote: "Your Lordship has gained considerable strength in your study of the Way.

As for the method of treating illness, you should seek deeply into the joy of Chan (Zen). Once the root of birth and death is pierced through, joy, anger, grief, and affliction will have no place to set foot.
